The union of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth) represents the hieros gamos, a recurring theme in mythology where sky and earth deities mate to produce offspring.
Gaia and Uranus produce twelve Titans: Oceanus, Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, Iapetus, Theia, Rhea, Themis, Mnemosyne, Phoebe, Tethys, and Cronus.
Gaia and Uranus produce the Cyclopes: Brontes, Steropes, and Arges, who have one eye in the middle of their foreheads and later fashion Zeus's thunderbolt.
Gaia and Uranus produce three hundred-armed, fifty-headed sons: Cottus, Briareus, and Gyes, who are hated by their father.
Oceanus and Tethys produce numerous children, the Oceanids: three thousand daughters and three thousand sons, spirits of rivers, waters, and springs.
Hyperion, a Titan sun-god, mates with Theia (or Euryphaëssa) to produce Helius (sun), Selene (moon), and Eos (dawn). Helius drives a chariot across the sky.

Earth (Ge) produces giants and Typhoeus to challenge Zeus. Zeus defeats the giants with the help of Heracles and imprisons them under the earth. Typhoeus, a hundred-headed dragon, is hurled into Tartarus after a fierce battle.

rel.desc: Prometheus is the creator of man in the creation myth.
Athena breathed life into the clay man.
Zeus is involved in the creation of mortals, sometimes as the sole creator.

myths.s: Hesiod describes five successive ages of humanity: Gold (under Cronus, carefree), Silver (foolish, destroyed by Zeus), Bronze (warlike, self-destroyed), Heroes (demigods who fought at Thebes and Troy, some sent to Islands of the Blessed), and Iron (current age of toil, wickedness, and eventual destruction by Zeus).

Prometheus, son of Iapetus, tricks Zeus at Mecone by dividing an ox unfairly. In retaliation, Zeus binds Prometheus and sends an eagle to eat his liver daily, which regenerates nightly. Heracles later kills the eagle and frees Prometheus, with Zeus's consent, to increase Heracles' fame.

Prometheus tricks Zeus by dividing a sacrificial ox into two portions: one with flesh and innards wrapped in paunch, the other with bones wrapped in fat. Zeus chooses the bones, establishing the practice of burning bones for the gods.

rel.desc: Prometheus tricks Zeus at Mecone.
Zeus is tricked by Prometheus at Mecone.

myths.s: After Zeus hides fire from mortals in anger at Prometheus' trick, Prometheus steals fire in a hollow fennel stalk and gives it to humans, angering Zeus further.

rel.desc: Prometheus steals fire from Zeus in this myth.
Zeus is angered by the theft of fire.

myths.s: As punishment for Prometheus' theft of fire, Zeus orders Hephaestus to create the first woman, Pandora, who is adorned by Athena and other gods. She is given to Epimetheus and brings a jar containing evils and hope; when opened, evils escape into the world, leaving only hope inside.

rel.desc: Pandora is the central figure in this myth.
Zeus orders the creation of Pandora.
Hephaestus fashions Pandora.
Athena adorns Pandora.
Epimetheus accepts Pandora as a gift.
Aphrodite bestows grace on Pandora.
Hermes gives Pandora a thievish nature and delivers her to Epimetheus.
The Graces adorn Pandora with golden necklaces.
Persuasion adorns Pandora with golden necklaces.
The Seasons crown Pandora with spring flowers.

myths.s: In Aeschylus' play, Prometheus is bound as punishment for giving fire to mortals. He claims to have given humans blind hopes to prevent them from foreseeing their fate.

rel.desc: Prometheus is the protagonist of Aeschylus' play.
Zeus is the antagonist in Prometheus Bound.

myths.s: Zeus (Jupiter) tests the wickedness of mortals in the Iron Age by becoming a man. He is angered by the evil of Lycaon and punishes him, leading to the decision to send a great flood.

rel.desc: Zeus punished Lycaon for his wickedness.
Zeus punishes Lycaon for serving human flesh by destroying his house and turning him into a wolf.
Zeus turns Lycaon into a wolf.
Lycaon is the father of Callisto.

myths.s: Zeus sends a great flood to punish mortals for their wickedness. Deucalion, son of Prometheus, and Pyrrha, daughter of Epimetheus, survive and repopulate the earth.
Jupiter decides to destroy humanity with a great flood instead of fire; Neptune aids by sending waves; only Deucalion and Pyrrha survive on Mount Parnassus.
After the flood, Deucalion and Pyrrha consult Themis, who tells them to throw the bones of their mother (stones) behind them; the stones turn into humans, repopulating the earth.
Zeus overthrows his father Cronus and the Titans, defeats the Giants and Prometheus, and slays the dragon Typhoeus to become supreme god.
Zeus kills the dragon Typhoeus, establishing himself as the archetypal dragonslayer.
Babylonian creation epic where Marduk defeats Tiamat, splits her body to create the sky and earth, and creates humans from the blood of Kingu.
Babylonian myth where Enlil creates humans to serve the gods, then sends a flood to destroy them, but Atrahasis survives with Enki's help.

rel.desc: Enlil sends the flood to destroy Atrahasis.
Ea advises Atrahasis to survive the flood.

myths.s: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, and his friend Enkidu kill Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven; after Enkidu's death, Gilgamesh seeks immortality and meets Ut-napishtim.
A great flood sent by Enlil to destroy humanity; survivors include Atrahasis, Ut-napishtim, Deucalion, and Noah.

myths.n: Sacred Marriage of Zeus and Hera
myths.s: Zeus and Hera enact the sacred marriage between sky-god and earth-goddess, described in Homer's Iliad where the earth sprouts new grass and flowers as they lie together under a golden cloud.

rel.desc: Zeus is a central figure in the Sacred Marriage myth.
Hera is a central figure in the Sacred Marriage myth.

rel.other: Zeus and Hera metope from Temple E at Selinus
rel.desc: The metope portrays the hieros gamos of Zeus and Hera.

myths.s: Hera, Poseidon, and Athena once bound Zeus in chains, but Thetis rescued him. This event is alluded to in the Iliad.

rel.desc: Zeus is the one bound in the Binding of Zeus myth.
Hera participates in binding Zeus.
Poseidon participates in binding Zeus.
Athena participates in binding Zeus.
Thetis rescues Zeus from being bound.

myths.s: Demeter's daughter Persephone was abducted by Hades, causing Demeter to grieve and refuse to let the earth bear fruit until Persephone was returned.

rel.desc: Demeter is the mother of Persephone and grieves her abduction.
Persephone is abducted by Hades.
Hades abducts Persephone.
Zeus is involved as father of Persephone and in negotiations.

myths.s: A brief hymn calling on Hestia as the personification of the protecting flame of the sacred hearth in a temple, asking her to enter the house with Zeus and grant grace to the song.

rel.desc: Hestia is the subject of the Homeric Hymn to Hestia (24).

myths.s: A hymn invoking Hestia as protectress of the hearth in the home, along with Hermes, asking them to inhabit beautiful homes in loving harmony.

rel.desc: Hestia is the subject of the Homeric Hymn to Hestia (29).
Hermes is invoked alongside Hestia in the Homeric Hymn to Hestia (29).

myths.s: Aphrodite proclaims she is the greatest deity, able to bend even Zeus to her amorous will, except for Athena, Artemis, and Hestia who defy her.

rel.desc: Aphrodite is the subject of the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite.
Zeus is mentioned as being subject to Aphrodite's power.

myths.s: Heracles was said to have founded the original Olympic Games, which were reorganized in 776 BCE with Zeus as principal god.

rel.desc: Zeus is the principal god of the Olympic Games.
Heracles founded the original Olympic Games.

myths.s: At the wedding of Pirithoüs and Hippodamia, centaurs got drunk and attempted to carry off the bride and other Lapith women, leading to a battle. The myth was depicted on the west pediment of the temple of Zeus at Olympia and in the metopes of the Parthenon.

myths.n: Chariot Race of Pelops and Hippodamia
myths.s: Pelops competed in a chariot race against Oenomaüs to win Hippodamia as his wife. The scene before the race is depicted on the east pediment of the temple of Zeus at Olympia, with Zeus as central figure guaranteeing Pelops' success.

Heracles performed twelve labors, including cleansing the stables of Augeas, capturing the Nemean Lion, and fetching Cerberus. These were carved in the metopes of the temple of Zeus at Olympia, with Athena and Hermes helping in some labors.
Apollo and Artemis killed the children of Niobe. This myth was depicted on the feet of the throne of Zeus at Olympia.
Heracles freed Prometheus, depicted on the screen enclosing the throne of Zeus at Olympia.
Zeus chose the handsome youth Ganymede to be cupbearer on Olympus, granting him immortality. The myth has been interpreted variously as a religious calling, a rape, or a joke.

rel.desc: Zeus loves Ganymede in a male homosexual relationship.
Ganymede was beloved by Zeus and made immortal.
Tros is the father of Ganymede.
Ganymede serves as cupbearer to Jupiter at the wedding feast.

myths.s: Zeus, in the form of a whirlwind or eagle, abducts the handsome Trojan prince Ganymede to be his cupbearer. He compensates Ganymede's father Tros with divine horses and grants Ganymede immortality.
Hephaestus, cast out of Olympus by Hera or Zeus, is brought back by Dionysus who makes him drunk. The scene is depicted on vases with Hephaestus on a donkey led by Dionysus and his retinue.
Zeus and Hera argue over Zeus's promise to Thetis to honor Achilles. Hephaestus intervenes, reminding them of his own fall from Olympus, and calms Hera by offering her a cup of nectar.
Thetis, mother of Achilles, supplicates Zeus to grant victory to the Trojans until the Greeks honor her son. Zeus agrees, nodding his head, which causes Olympus to tremble.
Hephaestus creates an elaborate shield for Achilles, described in detail in Homer's Iliad.

myths.n: The Love Affair of Ares and Aphrodite
myths.s: Hephaestus, learning from Helius that his wife Aphrodite is having an affair with Ares, forges an unbreakable net to trap them in bed. He summons the other gods to witness their shame, but Poseidon persuades him to release them. Ares flees to Thrace, and Aphrodite goes to Paphos where the Graces attend to her.

myths.n: Homeric Hymn to the Muses and Apollo
myths.s: A hymn invoking the Muses and Apollo, stating that through them humans become poets and musicians, and through Zeus they become kings. The Muses are praised as children of Zeus.

myths.n: Homeric Hymn to the Supreme Son of Cronus
myths.s: A hymn to Zeus, the best and greatest of gods, who confides his words of wisdom to Themis. It emphasizes Zeus's role as ruler and accomplisher.

myths.n: Story of the Daughters of Pierus
myths.s: Nine daughters of Pierus challenged the Muses to a musical contest, lost, and were turned into magpies.
Trophonius and Agamedes built the temple of Apollo at Delphi. When they asked for wages, Apollo said he would pay on the seventh day, and they fell asleep forever.
Cleobis and Biton, Argive brothers, died peacefully after a life of piety, similar to the story of Trophonius and Agamedes.

myths.n: The Meeting Between Solon and Croesus
myths.s: Solon visits Croesus and tells him that Tellus the Athenian is the happiest person, followed by Cleobis and Biton, who died peacefully after honoring their mother. Solon warns Croesus that wealth does not guarantee happiness until life ends well.

rel.desc: Tellus is mentioned as the happiest person by Solon.

myths.s: Croesus' son Atys dies, fulfilling a prophecy despite Croesus' attempts to avoid it. The story illustrates the interplay of fate and character.

rel.desc: Croesus is the main character in the story of Atys' death.
Atys is the son whose death is central to the story.

myths.s: Croesus, king of Lydia, is visited by Solon who warns him not to call anyone happy until death. Croesus ignores this. His son Atys is killed accidentally by Adrastus during a boar hunt, fulfilling a dream prophecy. Later, Croesus attacks Persia based on an ambiguous Delphic oracle, leading to his downfall. He is captured by Cyrus and placed on a pyre, but calls out Solon's name, prompting Cyrus to spare him.
Croesus, king of Lydia, learns from Solon that no man can be called happy until dead. He later attacks Persia, is captured by Cyrus, and is saved from burning by Apollo. He becomes Cyrus's counselor.
King Candaules of Lydia forces his bodyguard Gyges to see his wife naked. The wife, insulted, forces Gyges to kill Candaules and marry her, making Gyges king.
The musician Arion, thrown overboard by sailors, is saved by a dolphin that carries him to safety. He later confronts the sailors with Periander.

Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, throws his prized ring into the sea to avoid divine jealousy, but it is returned in a fish. His friend Amasis realizes his fate is sealed, and Polycrates is later murdered.
Annual festival honoring Athena Polias, involving a procession, presentation of a peplos embroidered with the Gigantomachy, sacrifice, and artistic representations on the Parthenon.
Orestes arrived in Athens after killing his mother; this myth was recalled during the Anthesteria festival.
Dionysus was killed and dismembered; this myth was recalled during the Anthesteria festival.
Icarius and his daughter Erigone were involved in a myth recalled during the Anthesteria festival.
Thetis was destined to bear a son mightier than his father, so Zeus avoided her. She married mortal Peleus, who caught her despite her shape-shifting. Their son Achilles became mightier than Peleus.

myths.n: Acis, Galatea, and the Cyclops Polyphemus
myths.s: The Cyclops Polyphemus loved the Nereid Galatea, but she loved Acis. Polyphemus killed Acis by throwing a rock, but Galatea transformed Acis into a river-god.
Poseidon won Amphitrite as his wife after she initially resisted. They had a son Triton. Poseidon had affairs, causing Amphitrite's jealousy.
Poseidon disguised himself as the river Enipeus and lay with Tyro, resulting in twins Neleus and Pelias.
Menelaüs, with help from Proteus' daughter Eidothea, consulted Proteus. Proteus changed shape but eventually answered Menelaüs' questions about his return home.
Scylla was transformed into a monster due to Amphitrite's or Circe's jealousy. She and Charybdis, a voracious daughter of Poseidon and Ge, terrorized the Straits of Messina.
Pontus and Ge produced Nereus, Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto, and Eurybië. Their descendants include many sea deities and monsters.
Poseidon and Athena competed for control of Athens and Attica. The story is associated with the west pediment of the Parthenon.

Galatea, a sea nymph, spurned the love of the Cyclops Polyphemus for the youth Acis. Polyphemus caught them together and crushed Acis under a rock, but Galatea transformed his blood into a river, making him a river-god.
Amphitrite, daughter of Nereus, initially spurned Neptune's advances but eventually became his consort. Poussin's painting depicts their triumph.
The hero Perseus beheaded the Gorgon Medusa, who was pregnant by Poseidon. From her corpse sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor.

myths.n: Heracles and the Apples of the Hesperides
myths.s: Heracles slew the dragon Ladon to steal the golden apples guarded by the Hesperides.
Heracles overcame the monster Geryon and his hound Orthus.
Heracles slew the Lernaean Hydra, a monster offspring of Echidna and Typhon.
Heracles killed the Nemean Lion, a monster offspring of Echidna and Orthus.

Athena was born from the head of Zeus, fully armed, after Zeus swallowed her mother Metis. Hephaestus (or Prometheus or Hermes) assisted by splitting Zeus's head. The event caused awe among the gods and cosmic disturbances.

rel.desc: Athena is the central figure in the myth of her own birth.
Zeus gives birth to Athena from his head.
Hephaestus assists in Athena's birth.
Prometheus sometimes assists in Athena's birth.
Hermes sometimes assists in Athena's birth.
Hera is probably present at Athena's birth on the Parthenon pediment.
Helius's horses appear on the east pediment of the Parthenon.
Selene's horses appear on the east pediment of the Parthenon.
Gaea advises Zeus to swallow Metis.
Uranus advises Zeus to swallow Metis.
Eileithyia assists at Athena's birth on the amphora.
Ares is present at Athena's birth on the amphora.
Apollo is present at Athena's birth on the amphora.

myths.s: Athena and Poseidon competed for control of Athens. Athena produced an olive tree with her spear, while Poseidon created a salt spring (or horse). Athena was declared victor by the gods, Athenians, or King Cecrops. Poseidon flooded the Thriasian plain in anger but was appeased.

rel.desc: Athena competes with Poseidon for Athens.
Zeus may have been involved in judging the contest.
Poseidon competes with Athena for Athens.
Cecrops judged the contest between Athena and Poseidon.
Erechtheus is associated with Poseidon in the Erechtheum.

myths.s: Athena was reared by Triton and had a playmate named Pallas. During a quarrel, Zeus intervened with the aegis, startling Pallas, and Athena accidentally killed her. In grief, Athena made a wooden image (the Palladium) which fell to Troy.

rel.desc: Athena accidentally kills Pallas.
Pallas is killed by Athena.
Triton is the father of Pallas and reared Athena.

myths.s: Arachne, a mortal weaver, boasted that her skill equaled Athena's. Athena (as Minerva) challenged her to a contest. Arachne wove a tapestry depicting the Rape of Europa, angering Athena, who struck her with a shuttle.

rel.desc: Athena challenges Arachne to a weaving contest.
Arachne challenges Athena to a weaving contest.
Idmon is the father of Arachne.

myths.s: Battle between Greeks and Amazons, depicted on the west metopes of the Parthenon and on the exterior of Athena's shield.

rel.desc: Athena is associated with the battle against the Amazons.

myths.s: Battle of the Lapiths and centaurs, depicted on the south metopes of the Parthenon and on Athena's sandals.

rel.desc: Athena is associated with the battle of Lapiths and centaurs.

myths.s: The destruction of Troy, depicted on the north metopes of the Parthenon.

rel.desc: Athena is associated with the sack of Troy.

myths.s: Arachne, a Lydian woman, challenges Athena to a weaving contest. Athena weaves scenes of gods punishing mortals, while Arachne weaves scenes of gods' amorous deceptions. Enraged by Arachne's success, Athena destroys her tapestry and strikes her. Arachne hangs herself, but Athena transforms her into a spider.

rel.desc: Athena competed with Arachne in a weaving contest.
Arachne is the daughter of Idmon of Colophon.
Arachne challenges Athena to a weaving contest.
Athena competed with Arachne in a weaving contest and punished her.
Athena transformed Arachne into a spider after she hanged herself.
Athena appears in the myth of Arachne.
Arachne is the central character in the myth of Arachne.
Arachne is the central character in the myth of Arachne.

myths.s: Athena sides with Apollo for the acquittal of Orestes, creating the court of the Areopagus and appeasing the Furies.

rel.desc: Athena appears in the Eumenides, part of the Oresteia.
Cilissa appears in Aeschylus' Oresteia.

myths.s: Pygmalion, disgusted by the prostitute women of Cyprus, sculpted an ivory statue of a woman and fell in love with it. He prayed to Venus, who brought the statue to life. They married and had a son, Paphos.

rel.desc: Aphrodite (Venus) answers Pygmalion's prayer and brings the statue to life.
Pygmalion married the statue brought to life, later named Galatea.
Pygmalion and Galatea had a son named Paphos.
Pygmalion is the protagonist of the Pygmalion myth.
Pygmalion is the protagonist of the Pygmalion myth.
Pygmalion loved the statue he created, which became Galatea.
Aphrodite granted Pygmalion's wish by animating the statue.

myths.s: Myrrha, daughter of Cinyras, committed incest with her father and was transformed into a myrrh tree, giving birth to Adonis. Aphrodite fell in love with Adonis, but he was killed by a boar while hunting.

rel.desc: Adonis is the lover of Aphrodite in this myth.

myths.s: Cybele, the Great Mother, falls in love with Attis. He loves another, and Cybele drives him mad; he castrates himself and dies. Cybele repents and obtains Zeus' promise that Attis' body will never decay.

Zeus causes Aphrodite to fall in love with the mortal Anchises as revenge for her boasts. The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite describes her power and her union with Anchises, who fears debilitation from sleeping with a goddess.

rel.desc: Anchises is a key character in the myth.
Zeus instigates the myth by putting desire in Aphrodite.
Aeneas is prophesied to be born from the union.
Hermes escorts Aphrodite to Anchises.

myths.s: In Plato's Symposium, Aristophanes explains that humans originally had three sexes (male, female, and androgynous) and were spherical with four arms and four legs. They attacked the gods, so Zeus split them in half, causing humans to seek their other half. Eros is the desire to reunite with one's original other half.

Aristophanes explains the origin of love by recounting a myth where humans were originally spherical beings with two faces, four arms, and four legs. Zeus split them in two as punishment for their insolence, and Apollo healed them. Now each half longs for its other half, and love is the desire for wholeness.

Socrates, instructed by Diotima, argues that Eros is not a god but a great spirit intermediate between gods and humans. Eros is neither good nor bad, beautiful nor ugly, but a lover of wisdom who seeks the good and the beautiful.

rel.desc: Alcibiades appears in the Symposium and tells of his attempts to seduce Socrates.
Plato wrote the Symposium, which contains Socrates' speech.

myths.s: A king and queen have three daughters; the youngest, Psyche, is so beautiful that Venus becomes jealous. Venus orders Cupid to make Psyche fall in love with a monster, but Cupid falls in love with her instead. Psyche is left on a mountaintop as a bride for a serpent, but Zephyrus carries her to Cupid's palace. After trials and labors, she is united with Cupid.

rel.desc: Psyche is the main character in the myth of Cupid and Psyche.
Venus appears in the myth of Cupid and Psyche.
Apollo appears in the myth of Cupid and Psyche.
Zephyrus appears in the myth of Cupid and Psyche.
Apuleius gave the classic form to the story of Cupid and Psyche in his Metamorphoses.
The story of Cupid and Psyche is contained in Apuleius' Metamorphoses.
The painting by Jacques-Louis David depicts the myth of Cupid and Psyche.

myths.s: Leto, impregnated by Zeus, gives birth to the twin deities Artemis and Apollo on the island of Delos. Artemis is born first and helps deliver Apollo. Hera's anger forces Leto to wander; in Lycia, she turns inhospitable Lycians into frogs.

rel.desc: Artemis is born and helps deliver Apollo.
Apollo is born after Artemis.
Leto gives birth to Artemis and Apollo.
Zeus is the father of Artemis and Apollo.
Hera's anger causes Leto to wander.

myths.s: Niobe, queen of Thebes, boasts that she is more deserving of worship than Leto because she has seven sons and seven daughters. Leto complains to Artemis and Apollo, who kill all of Niobe's children with arrows. Niobe is turned to stone and placed on a mountaintop in Phrygia, where she weeps eternally.

rel.desc: Artemis kills Niobe's daughters in the myth.
Apollo kills Niobe's sons in the myth.
Niobe is the central mortal character in the myth.
Leto is insulted by Niobe and complains to her children.

myths.s: The hunter Actaeon accidentally stumbles upon Artemis bathing naked in a cave. In anger, Artemis splashes water on him, transforming him into a stag. His own hunting hounds, not recognizing him, chase and tear him apart.

rel.desc: Artemis transforms Actaeon into a stag after he sees her naked.
Actaeon is the protagonist of the myth.
Actaeon is the protagonist of the myth.
Cadmus is the grandfather of Actaeon, mentioned in the myth.
Autonoë is the mother of Actaeon.
Artemis transforms Actaeon into a stag.
Actaeon is killed by his own hounds after Artemis transforms him.
Actaeon accidentally saw Artemis bathing, leading to his punishment.
Artemis punished Actaeon for seeing her bathing.
Aristaeus is the father of Actaeon.
Autonoë is the mother of Actaeon.
Actaeon is mentioned as the son of Autonoë in The Bacchae.
Actaeon is the son of Autonoë.
Actaeon and Dionysus are cousins (through Cadmus).
Actaeon and Pentheus are cousins (through Cadmus).

myths.s: Actaeon accidentally sees Artemis bathing; as punishment, she transforms him into a stag, and he is torn apart by his own hounds.

Jupiter seduces Callisto by disguising as Diana; Callisto becomes pregnant and is expelled by Diana; Juno transforms her into a bear; her son Arcas nearly kills her but Jupiter turns them into constellations.
Orion, a mighty hunter, woos Merope, is blinded by Oenopion, regains sight via Helius, attempts to rape Artemis, and is killed by a scorpion sent by her; he and his dog become constellations.

rel.desc: Eos loved Orion.
Orion attempted to rape Artemis.
Artemis sent a scorpion to kill Orion.
Orion wooed Merope.
Oenopion blinded Orion.
Helius restored Orion's sight.
Orion pursued the Pleiades.

myths.s: The river-god Alpheus pursues the nymph Arethusa; she prays to Artemis, who transforms her into a stream that flows underground to Syracuse.

rel.desc: Alpheus loved Arethusa and pursued her.
Arethusa was a follower of Artemis.
Artemis transformed Arethusa into a stream.

myths.s: Aphrodite, angered by Hippolytus' devotion to Artemis and rejection of love, causes his stepmother Phaedra to fall in love with him. Phaedra's nurse reveals the secret to Hippolytus, who is horrified. Phaedra commits suicide and leaves a note falsely accusing Hippolytus of rape. Theseus curses Hippolytus, leading to his death. Artemis appears to the dying Hippolytus, promising vengeance and establishing a cult in his honor.

rel.desc: Hippolytus is devoted to Artemis and rejects Aphrodite.
Aphrodite is enraged because Hippolytus spurns her.
Phaedra falls in love with her stepson Hippolytus.
Theseus is the father of Hippolytus.
Artemis appears to the dying Hippolytus.
Artemis promises to avenge Hippolytus by harming a favorite of Aphrodite.
Hippolytus was brought up by Pittheus.
Hippolytus is the son of Theseus.
Hippolytus is a devotee of Artemis, the virgin goddess.
The Nurse reveals Phaedra's love to Hippolytus.
Theseus curses Hippolytus using one of Poseidon's granted curses.
Phaedra leaves a note falsely accusing Hippolytus of rape.
Hippolytus rejects the worship of Aphrodite, leading to her vengeance.
Aphrodite hates Hippolytus because he renounces her.
Aphrodite is angry at Hippolytus and causes his destruction.
Poseidon sent a bull that caused Hippolytus' death, fulfilling Theseus' curse.
The Nurse revealed Phaedra's love to Hippolytus under oath.
Hippolytus was sworn to secrecy by the Nurse.
Phaedra falsely accused Hippolytus of rape in her suicide note.
Hippolytus rejected Phaedra's advances.
Theseus cursed Hippolytus using one of three curses from Poseidon.
Theseus cursed Hippolytus, leading to his death.
Hippolytus is Artemis' huntsman and servant.
Artemis says Hippolytus is 'most dear' to her.
Hippolytus renounced Aphrodite and her domain.
Hippolytus swore by Zeus god of oaths that he was innocent.
Asclepius restored Hippolytus to life at Artemis's request.
Hippolytus is the son of Theseus and Antiope.
Hippolytus was falsely accused by Phaedra.
Artemis assured Hippolytus of future honor and he was closely connected with her.
Hippolytus was connected with Aphrodite at Athens, where her temple was called 'Aphrodite by Hippolytus'.
Asclepius brought Hippolytus back to life.
Hippolytus in his resurrected form was absorbed by the Italians with the name Virbius.

myths.s: Callisto, a follower of Artemis, is seduced by Zeus and transformed into a bear. She becomes the constellation Ursa Major.

rel.desc: Callisto was a follower of Artemis.
Jupiter seduced Callisto, resulting in pregnancy.
Callisto is the mother of Arcas.
Juno was vengeful against Callisto for her affair with Jupiter.
Lycaon is the father of Callisto.
Zeus seduced Callisto by taking the form of Artemis.
Callisto was a follower of Artemis.

myths.s: Niobe, wife of Amphion, boasts of her many children, angering Leto, who sends Apollo and Artemis to kill them. Niobe is turned to stone on Mount Sipylus.

rel.desc: Niobe is the central mortal character in the myth.
Niobe boasted against Leto, leading to her punishment.
Tantalus is the father of Niobe.
Atlas is the grandfather of Niobe.
Amphion is the husband of Niobe.
Apollo acted against Niobe for her boasting.
Niobe is mentioned as Amphion's wife.
Niobe is daughter of Phoroneus.
Apis is son of Niobe and Zeus.

myths.s: Artemis is born on Delos (or Ortygia) to Leto and Zeus, assisting in the birth of her twin brother Apollo.

Leto, pregnant with Apollo and Artemis, wanders seeking a place to give birth. Delos agrees to accept Apollo after Leto swears an oath that Apollo will build his temple there. After nine days of labor, with the help of Eileithyia, Apollo is born on Delos under a palm tree. Themis feeds him nectar and ambrosia, and Apollo immediately declares his domains: lyre, bow, and prophecy.

Delos becomes the sacred island of Apollo, site of his important sanctuary. The Homeric Hymn describes the festival at Delos with the Deliades maidens singing. The story of Anius, son of Apollo, is also associated with Delos.

Anius, king of Delos, had three daughters who received from Dionysus the power to produce oil, grain, and wine. Agamemnon tried to force them to go to Troy, but they resisted and were turned into white doves by Dionysus.

The Homeric Hymn to Apollo describes Apollo's descent from Olympus, his journey through Greece, and his foundation of the oracle at Delphi after slaying the she-dragon Python. It also tells how Apollo recruited Cretan sailors as his attendants by transforming into a dolphin.
Apollo slew a she-dragon at Crisa near Parnassus, and the site was called Pytho because the sun made the monster rot. This act represents Apollo's conquest of the earlier earth-goddess oracle.

Zeus released two eagles from opposite ends of the earth; they met at Delphi, marking it as the center of the earth. Apollo established his oracle there after slaying the dragon and recruiting Cretan sailors.
Apollo transformed into a dolphin and leaped aboard a Cretan ship, forcing the sailors to follow him to Crisa. He revealed himself as a god and appointed them as attendants at his sanctuary.

The Pythia, Apollo's prophetess, delivered oracles from the tripod in the adyton. Inquirers underwent purification and sacrifices before consulting the god. The oracle was active nine months a year and was known for ambiguous responses.

The Cumaean Sibyl, a prophetess of Apollo, guides Aeneas in the underworld. She prophesies in a cavern with a hundred mouths, and her prophecies are sometimes written on leaves that scatter. Apollo loved her and granted her long life, but she forgot to ask for eternal youth, so she ages and eventually becomes a tiny voice.
Apollo loved Cassandra, daughter of Priam, and gave her the power of prophecy. When she rejected him, he spat into her mouth, ensuring that no one would ever believe her prophecies.
Apollo and Idas both wooed Marpessa. Idas carried her off, and Apollo stole her back. Zeus ordered Marpessa to choose; she chose Idas, fearing Apollo would abandon her when she grew old.
Apollo fell in love with the athletic nymph Cyrene while watching her wrestle a lion. He took her to Libya, where the city Cyrene was named after her, and she bore him a son, Aristaeus.

Apollo loves Coronis, who is pregnant with his child. A raven reports her infidelity; Apollo kills her with an arrow but repents. He saves his son Asclepius from the funeral pyre and gives him to Chiron to raise.

Marsyas, a satyr, picked up the flute discarded by Athena and became so proficient that he challenged Apollo to a musical contest. Apollo won and flayed Marsyas alive. The satyr's tears formed the river Marsyas in Phrygia.

Pan challenged Apollo to a musical contest, with Tmolus as judge. Tmolus judged Apollo the winner, but Midas disagreed. Apollo gave Midas ass's ears as punishment. Midas's barber revealed the secret by whispering into a hole, and reeds grew that spread the story.

Apollo, in exile for killing the Cyclopes, served King Admetus. He obtained longer life for Admetus from the Moirai on condition that someone die in his place. Admetus's wife Alcestis volunteered, but Heracles rescued her from death by wrestling Thanatos.

rel.desc: Admetus married Alcestis.
Alcestis sacrificed her life so that Admetus could live longer.
Heracles rescued Alcestis from death by wrestling Thanatos.

myths.s: Asclepius, a skilled physician, restored Hippolytus to life at Artemis's request. Zeus, angered by this disruption of nature, struck Asclepius with a thunderbolt and hurled him into the underworld.
Apollo, angered by the insult to his priest Chryses, descends from Olympus and shoots plague arrows at the Greek camp, causing mass death.

myths.n: Apollo Seeks a Site for His Oracle
myths.s: Apollo travels over the earth seeking a location for his oracle. He eventually chooses Delphi, where he slays the Python.
The hymn describes Apollo's arrival at Olympus, where he plays the lyre and the gods dance and sing. It also mentions his love affairs and his search for an oracle site.
Apollo slays the serpent Python at Delphi, thereby taking possession of the site for his oracle.

myths.n: Apollo's Search for a Temple Site
myths.s: Apollo searches for a location to build his temple and oracle. He rejects several sites, is deceived by Telphusa, and finally chooses Crisa beneath Mt. Parnassus, where he builds his temple at Delphi.
Apollo kills the she-dragon at Delphi with his bow. The monster had been raised by Hera and had caused harm to mortals. After her death, the place is called Pytho, and Apollo is titled Pythian.

Angry at Zeus for giving birth to Athena alone, Hera prays to Earth and the Titans for a child stronger than Zeus. She gives birth to Typhaon, a terrible monster, whom she gives to the she-dragon to raise.
Apollo, in the form of a dolphin, leaps onto a Cretan ship and guides it to Crisa. The Cretans become his priests at Delphi.

Apollo, in the form of a dolphin, guides a Cretan ship to Crisa, where he establishes his temple at Delphi. He reveals himself as Apollo, son of Zeus, and appoints the Cretans as his priests, instructing them to worship him as Delphinius and to sing the Ie Paean.

rel.desc: Apollo is the central figure in this hymn.
The Cretans are the human characters in this hymn.
Helius is mentioned as having sheep at Taenarum.

myths.s: Apollo slew the dragon Python at Delphi, establishing his sanctuary there. The festival Stepteria commemorated this event every ninth year.
The satyr Marsyas challenged Apollo to a musical contest. After Apollo won, he flayed Marsyas alive for his hubris.
Zeus fathers Hermes with Maia in a cave, without the knowledge of Hera. Hermes is born on the fourth day of the month and quickly shows his cleverness.

Maia is the mother of Hermes in this myth.
Zeus fathers Hermes in this myth.

myths.s: Shortly after birth, Hermes finds a tortoise, kills it, and fashions the first lyre from its shell, using reeds, oxhide, and sheep gut strings. He sings of Zeus and Maia.

rel.desc: Hermes invents the lyre in this myth.

myths.s: Hermes steals fifty cattle from Apollo, reversing their tracks to confuse pursuit. He invents fire sticks, sacrifices two cows, and hides the meat. He returns to his cradle and confronts his mother Maia, vowing to gain honor.

rel.desc: Hermes steals Apollo's cattle in this myth.
Apollo's cattle are stolen by Hermes.
Helius is descending when Hermes steals the cattle.
Selene's light shines during Hermes' theft.
Hephaestus' power kindles the fire for Hermes' sacrifice.

myths.s: Hermes steals fifty cows from Apollo's herd, driving them backward to confuse pursuit. He hides them in a cave near Pylos. Apollo, with the help of an old man and a bird omen, tracks Hermes to his cave. After a dispute, Zeus reconciles them, and Hermes gives Apollo the lyre in exchange for the cattle.

rel.desc: Hermes is the main actor in the myth of the cattle theft.
Apollo is the victim and pursuer in the myth.
Zeus judges the dispute between Hermes and Apollo.
Maia is present in the cave when Apollo confronts Hermes.

myths.s: A Homeric hymn that tells the story of Hermes' birth, his invention of the lyre, theft of Apollo's cattle, and reconciliation with Apollo. It highlights Hermes' cleverness and the establishment of his roles as messenger, god of herds, and guide to the underworld.

rel.desc: Hermes is the central figure in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
Apollo appears in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
Zeus appears in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
Maia appears in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.

The Muses are mentioned in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
Hades is mentioned in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
Cronus is mentioned in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
Argus is mentioned in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
The holy sisters appear in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.

myths.s: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes describes the birth and early exploits of Hermes, including his theft of Apollo's cattle and invention of the lyre.

The nymph Salmacis falls in love with Hermaphroditus, son of Hermes and Aphrodite. When he rejects her, she prays to be united with him forever, and their bodies merge into one being with both male and female attributes.

rel.desc: Hermaphroditus is the main character in the myth.
Salmacis is the nymph in the myth.
Alcithoë tells the story of Hermaphroditus and Salmacis to her sisters.

myths.s: Zeus had an affair with Semele, a daughter of Cadmus. Hera, jealous, tricked Semele into asking Zeus to appear in his divine form, which killed her. Zeus saved the unborn Dionysus and sewed him into his thigh, from which he was later born. Hermes took the infant to the nymphs of Nysa to be raised.

rel.desc: Dionysus is the central figure in the myth of his birth.
Zeus plays a key role in the birth of Dionysus.
Semele is the mother of Dionysus in the birth myth.
Hera's jealousy leads to Semele's death in the birth myth.
Hermes rescues and carries the infant Dionysus.
Ino cares for the infant Dionysus.
Kore (Persephone) is the mother of Dionysus.
Titans dismember and devour Dionysus.

myths.s: Dionysus returns to Thebes to establish his worship and punish his mother's sisters for denying his divinity. He drives the women of Thebes mad, including his aunts, and confronts King Pentheus, who opposes him. The play explores the power and terror of Dionysian worship.

rel.desc: Dionysus is the main character in Euripides' play The Bacchae.
Pentheus is a character in The Bacchae.
Cadmus appears in The Bacchae.
Semele is mentioned in The Bacchae.

Echion is mentioned as the father of Pentheus in The Bacchae.
Agenor is mentioned as the father of Cadmus in The Bacchae.
Cybele is mentioned as the great mother in the Bacchic context.
Rhea is mentioned as the mother-goddess associated with the drum.
Curetes are mentioned as attendants of Zeus on Crete.
Corybantes are mentioned as inventors of the drum and flutes.
Satyrs are mentioned as taking up the drum from Rhea.

Aphrodite is mentioned in the context of women's lust.
Pentheus is the central mortal in the myth of The Bacchae.
Dionysus is the central god in the myth of The Bacchae.

myths.s: Dionysus danced with Ariadne, kissed her, and they embraced. The audience watched excitedly as they kissed and moved off to their marriage bed, inspiring others to marry.

rel.desc: Dionysus is the groom in the reenactment of his marriage to Ariadne.
Ariadne is the bride in the reenactment.

myths.s: The daughters of King Proetus of Tiryns resisted Dionysus and were driven mad, rushing over the countryside and killing their children. The seer Melampus cured them with herbs and therapeutic dances, though one daughter, Iphinoë, died during the pursuit.

The daughters of Minyas of Orchomenus refused to participate in Bacchic worship and were driven mad. Leucippe's son Hippasus was torn to pieces. The Minyads were transformed into winged creatures of the night (owls or bats).
Lycurgus of Thrace pursued the nurses of Dionysus with an ox goad. Dionysus jumped into the sea in terror and was rescued by Thetis. Zeus struck Lycurgus with blindness and he died soon after.

rel.desc: Zeus struck Lycurgus with blindness and he died soon after.
Lycurgus pursued the nurses of Dionysus.
Opheltes is son of Lycurgus.

myths.s: A hymn describing the birth of Dionysus, sewn in Zeus' thigh, born on Mount Nysa near Egypt. It establishes the universal power of his worship and triennial festivals.
A hymn describing Dionysus as ivy-crowned and loud-crying, nurtured by nymphs in the vales of Mount Nysa. He wanders in the forest with nymphs following him.
Silenus, made drunk by wine-laced water, was brought to King Midas. He philosophized that the best fate for humans is not to be born, and the next best is to die soon after birth.
Dionysus married Ariadne after she was deserted by Theseus on Naxos, symbolizing the union of male and female vegetation powers and Dionysus' redemptive power.

Zeus mated with Persephone, who bore Zagreus (Dionysus). Hera aroused the Titans to attack the child; they dismembered and devoured him. Athena saved his heart, and Zeus destroyed the Titans with thunder. From the Titans' ashes, humans were born, giving them a dual nature: evil body from Titans, divine soul from the devoured god.

Icarius was hospitable to Dionysus and received wine as a gift. People thought they were poisoned and killed Icarius. His daughter Erigone searched for him and hanged herself. Plague ensued until, on Apollo's advice, a festival was initiated in their honor.

Silenus was captured and brought to King Midas, who returned him to Dionysus. As a reward, Midas was granted the golden touch. He soon regretted it when he could not eat or drink. Dionysus ordered him to wash in the river Pactolus, which then had golden sands.

Pirates abducted Dionysus, mistaking him for a mortal. Miracles occurred: wine flowed, vines grew, and the god transformed into a lion and bear. The pirates jumped into the sea and became dolphins. The helmsman was saved.
Pan pursued the nymph Syrinx, who was transformed into marsh reeds. The wind blowing through the reeds produced a sound, inspiring Pan to create the panpipe.
Pan loved the nymph Echo, but she fled from him. Pan caused madness among shepherds, who tore Echo to pieces. Only her voice remained.
Pan was born to Hermes and Dryope, daughter of Dryops. He is goat-footed, two-horned, and loves music.

Echo, cursed by Juno to only repeat words, fell in love with Narcissus but was rejected. Narcissus then fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and wasted away, eventually dying. The story includes the prophecy of Tiresias and the prayer of a scorned lover answered by Nemesis.

rel.desc: Pan is mentioned in the context of Echo's story.

myths.s: Narcissus, a beautiful youth, rejected the love of the nymph Echo, who pined away until only her voice remained. As punishment, Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection in a pool, and unable to attain it, he died and was transformed into a flower.

Persephone is abducted by Hades while picking flowers in a meadow, with Zeus's consent. Demeter searches for her, learns the truth from Helius, and in grief withdraws from the gods, causing the earth to become barren.

rel.desc: Persephone is the central figure in the abduction myth.
Demeter is a main character in the abduction myth.
Hades is the abductor in the myth.
Zeus arranges the compromise for Persephone's return.
Hermes is sent to retrieve Persephone from the Underworld.
Hecate accompanies Persephone and becomes her attendant.
Rhea is sent by Zeus to reconcile Demeter.

myths.s: Demeter, disguised as an old woman, comes to Eleusis and is taken in by the family of King Celeus. She becomes nurse to their baby son, but her identity is eventually revealed.

rel.desc: Demeter is the main character in the Eleusis episode.
Celeus hosts Demeter in Eleusis.

myths.s: Demeter, disguised as a nurse, anoints Demophoön with ambrosia and places him in the fire at night to make him immortal. Metaneira interrupts, causing Demeter to reveal herself and stop the process.

Zeus sends Hermes to retrieve Persephone from Hades. Hades allows her to leave but tricks her into eating pomegranate seeds, ensuring her return each year. Demeter and Persephone are reunited, and the earth becomes fertile again.

After restoring fertility, Demeter teaches her sacred rites to the kings of Eleusis, including Triptolemus, establishing the Eleusinian Mysteries. Initiates who witness these rites are promised a blessed afterlife.

rel.desc: Triptolemus is taught the mysteries and spreads agriculture.
Celeus is one of the kings taught the mysteries.
Metaneira interferes with Demeter's attempt to make Demophoön immortal.
Demophoön is the infant nursed by Demeter.
Diocles is one of the kings taught the mysteries.
Eumolpus is one of the kings taught the mysteries.
Polyxeinus is one of the kings taught the mysteries.
Demeter establishes the mysteries at Eleusis.
Persephone is honored alongside Demeter in the mysteries.

myths.s: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter recounts the abduction of Persephone by Hades, Demeter's grief and wanderings, her stay at Eleusis, and the eventual reunion with her daughter, which restores fertility to the earth.

rel.desc: Demeter is the main character of the Hymn to Demeter.
Persephone's abduction is central to the Hymn to Demeter.
Demophoön appears in the Hymn to Demeter in a traumatic episode.

myths.s: The Eleusinian Mysteries were secret religious rites held annually at Eleusis, involving initiation stages (Lesser and Greater Mysteries), processions, purification, and a dramatic reenactment of Demeter's story, culminating in the revelation of sacred objects.
Myth of Zagreus-Dionysus, son of Persephone, who was dismembered and reborn, providing authority for Orphism.

Odysseus travels to the Underworld to consult the seer Tiresias about his return to Ithaca. He performs sacrifices, speaks with the shades of the dead including his mother Anticlea, and encounters heroes like Achilles and Ajax.

Odysseus visits the Underworld, where he sees the souls of the dead, including Minos, Orion, Tityus, Tantalus, Sisyphus, and Heracles. He also encounters his mother Anticlea and heroes like Agamemnon and Achilles.

Sisyphus, son of Aeolus, outwits Death by chaining him, preventing mortals from dying. After Ares frees Death, Sisyphus tricks Hades by instructing his wife not to make sacrifices, allowing him to return to Corinth. He is eventually punished in the Underworld by rolling a rock uphill forever.

Er, a Pamphylian, dies in war and returns to life after twelve days. He describes the afterlife: souls are judged and travel through openings in earth and sky, undergoing a thousand-year cycle of punishment and reward.

rel.desc: Er is the central figure and narrator of the Myth of Er.
Ardiaeus is mentioned as a tyrant being punished in the afterlife.
Necessity is described as the mother of the Fates and holder of the spindle.
Sirens are perched on the circles of the spindle, producing harmony.
Lachesis is one of the Fates who assigns lots and lives to souls.
Clotho helps turn the spindle and sings of the present.
Atropos moves the inner circles and sings of the future.
Orpheus's soul chooses the life of a swan.
Thamyras's soul selects the life of a nightingale.
Ajax's soul chooses the life of a lion.
Agamemnon's soul changes to the life of an eagle.
Atalanta's soul takes the life of a male athlete.
Epeus's soul assumes the nature of a craftswoman.
Thersites's soul takes the form of an ape.
Odysseus's soul chooses the quiet life of an ordinary man.
Plato recounts the Myth of Er in The Republic.

myths.s: Orpheus visits the Underworld to retrieve his wife Eurydice, playing music before Pluto and Proserpina.
Heracles captures Cerberus, the three-headed dog guarding the Underworld, as one of his labors.
Aeneas, guided by the Sibyl, visits the Underworld with the golden bough.
Dante's epic poem describing a journey through Hell, combining classical myths with medieval Christian doctrine.

Aeneas, guided by the Sibyl, descends to the Underworld to visit his father. He must obtain the golden bough and bury Misenus. They encounter various monsters, cross the Styx with Charon, and see unburied souls like Palinurus.

rel.desc: Vergil describes Aeneas' journey in Book 6 of the Aeneid.

myths.s: Aeneas, guided by the Sibyl, descends to the Underworld to visit his father Anchises. They encounter Charon, Cerberus, various souls, and the realms of Tartarus and Elysium, witnessing punishments and rewards.

Ixion, son of Phlegyas, killed his father-in-law Eïoneus and was purified by Zeus. He then attempted to violate Hera, but Zeus deceived him with a cloud (Nephele), who bore Centaurus. Ixion was punished by being bound to a winged wheel that rolls eternally.
Aristophanes' comedy in which Dionysus rows across the Styx to the Underworld, accompanied by a chorus of frogs croaking 'brekekekex koax koax'. It is a humorous tour of the Underworld.
Satirical dialogues by Lucian that portray the Underworld in varied moods.

Orpheus marries Eurydice, but she dies from a snake bite. Orpheus descends to the underworld and charms Hades and Persephone with his music, winning permission to bring Eurydice back on condition he not look back until they reach the upper world. He fails and loses her forever.

rel.desc: Orpheus is the main character in the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice.
Eurydice is the main character in the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice.
Hermes leads Eurydice back to the Underworld.

myths.s: After losing Eurydice, Orpheus shuns women and turns to love of young men. Ciconian maenads, angered by his rejection, attack him during a Bacchic frenzy, tearing him apart. His head and lyre float down the river Hebrus to Lesbos, where Apollo turns a snake to stone. His shade reunites with Eurydice in the underworld.
Orpheus was a member of Jason's expedition to retrieve the Golden Fleece.

rel.desc: Orpheus was a member of the Argonautic expedition.
Jason led the Argonautic expedition.

myths.s: Orpheus is killed by Thracian women, either because he neglected them, refused to initiate them, or enticed their husbands away. In some versions, he is struck by Zeus' thunderbolt or killed by followers of Dionysus. His head and lyre are taken to Lesbos, where his head becomes an oracle.

rel.desc: Orpheus is the subject of the myth of his death.
Dionysus is involved in the death of Orpheus.
Apollo suppressed the prophecies from Orpheus' head.
Zeus struck down Orpheus with a thunderbolt.

myths.s: The Orphic creation myth begins with Chronus (Time) and Adrasteia (Necessity). From Chronus comes Aether, Chaos, and Erebus. An egg is formed from which Phanes emerges. Phanes creates Night, who bears Gaea and Uranus. Cronus succeeds, then Zeus. Zeus swallows Phanes and recreates everything. Zeus mates with Persephone to produce Dionysus.

Cronus succeeds Night.

Kore (Persephone) mates with Zeus to produce Dionysus.

myths.s: Mithras slays a bull, from whose blood springs fertility; central to Mithraic iconography.
Isis searches for her husband/brother Osiris, dismembered by Seth, and for her child Horus.
Lucius, transformed into a donkey, prays to Isis; she appears in a dream and instructs him to take a garland of roses from a priest, restoring his human form.
Cadmus, son of Agenor, was sent to find his sister Europa after her abduction. He founded the city of Thebes, whose citadel was named Cadmeia after him.

rel.desc: Cadmus is the protagonist in the founding of Thebes.

myths.s: The saga of Thebes, centered on the cursed family of Labdacus, including Oedipus and Antigone, as treated by Sophocles.
Zeus, disguised as a bull, abducted Europa from Phoenicia and took her to Crete, where she became mother of Minos.

rel.desc: Europa is the central figure in the myth of her abduction.
The Selinus metope depicts the abduction of Europa.
Titian's painting depicts the abduction of Europa.

myths.s: Laius abducted Chrysippus, son of Pelops, in a chariot, as depicted on an Apulian bell-krater.

rel.desc: Laius is the abductor in the myth of Chrysippus.
Chrysippus is the victim in the abduction myth.
The Apulian bell-krater depicts the abduction of Chrysippus.

myths.s: Antiope gives birth to twin sons Amphion and Zethus, who are left to die but found by a shepherd. They later recognize their mother, avenge her by killing Lycus and Dirce, and become rulers of Cadmeia. Amphion builds the city walls with his lyre's music, and the city is renamed Thebes after Zethus' wife.

Zethus is a central character in the myth of Amphion and Zethus.

myths.s: Oedipus, after unknowingly killing his father Laius, comes to Thebes and solves the riddle of the Sphinx, freeing the city. He becomes king and marries his mother Jocasta, fulfilling the prophecy.

Pelops' curse is part of the background to the myth.
Chrysippus is mentioned in the background of the myth.

Laius is killed by Oedipus before the Sphinx episode.

Merope is Oedipus' adoptive mother.
Apollo's oracle foretold the fate of Oedipus.

myths.s: Years later, a plague afflicts Thebes. Oedipus discovers the truth about his parentage and crimes: he killed his father and married his mother. Jocasta hangs herself, and Oedipus blinds himself. Creon becomes regent, and Oedipus is banished.

Laius is the murdered king whose killer is sought.

myths.s: Oedipus, after years of wandering, arrives at Colonus with Antigone. He is protected by Theseus and the Eumenides, defends his innocence, curses his son Polynices, and dies a miraculous death, becoming a hero.

Antigone appears in Oedipus at Colonus.

Polynices appears in Oedipus at Colonus.

myths.s: Oedipus unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother, fulfilling Apollo's prophecy. He discovers the truth and blinds himself.

rel.desc: Oedipus is the protagonist of Oedipus Tyrannus.
Jocasta appears in Oedipus Tyrannus.

myths.s: Antigone defies Creon's decree to bury her brother Polynices, upholding unwritten laws, and dies as a result.

myths.s: Pelops sought to marry Hippodamia, daughter of King Oenomaüs, who challenged suitors to a chariot race. With help from Poseidon (who gave him a golden chariot) or by bribing Myrtilus to sabotage Oenomaüs' chariot, Pelops won the race and married Hippodamia.
