myths.s: Philoctetes was bitten by a snake and abandoned on Lemnos due to his wound's stench. Later, Odysseus and Diomedes fetched him after Helenus prophesied that Heracles' bow and arrows were needed to capture Troy.
Achilles wounded Telephus, son of Heracles, in Mysia. Later, Telephus was healed by Achilles, possibly with rust from the spear.

rel.desc: Achilles wounded and later healed Telephus.

myths.s: Telephus, wounded by Achilles' spear, was told by the Delphic oracle that 'he that wounded shall heal.' He went to the Greek army disguised as a beggar, and scrapings from Achilles' spear healed him.

rel.desc: Telephus is the son of Heracles.
Achilles wounded Telephus in battle.
Telephus was wounded by Achilles' spear.
Achilles healed Telephus by applying scrapings from his spear.
Telephus was a son of Heracles.

myths.s: Protesilaüs, the first Greek to leap ashore at Troy, was killed by Hector. His wife Laodamia grieved so much that Hermes brought him back from Hades for a few hours; when he was taken again, she killed herself.

The Iliad covers events from the quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon to the ransoming and burial of Hector. Agamemnon takes Briseïs from Achilles, causing Achilles to withdraw from battle. The Greeks suffer, and the Trojans gain success. Key episodes include the duel between Menelaüs and Paris, and Hector's farewell to Andromache.
Achilles and Agamemnon quarrel over Briseïs, leading Achilles to withdraw from battle.
Patroclus is killed by Hector while wearing Achilles' armor.
Thetis obtains new armor from Hephaestus for Achilles, including the famous shield.
Achilles ends his quarrel, receives Briseïs and new armor, and returns to fight Hector.
Achilles fights the river-god Scamander, filling the river with Trojan corpses.
Achilles kills Hector after chasing him around Troy, with Athena's help.
Achilles holds funeral games and sacrifices Trojan prisoners on Patroclus' pyre.
Priam ransoms Hector's body from Achilles, leading to a moment of compassion.
The Trojans mourn Hector for nine days; Andromache, Hecuba, and Helen lament.
Odysseus and others try to persuade Achilles to return to battle.
Gods fight each other on the battlefield in two episodes (Iliad Books 5 and 20-21), highlighting the gap between mortal and divine.
Diomedes wounds Aphrodite in battle; she returns to Olympus and is comforted by her mother Dione.
Diomedes wounds Ares, who complains to Zeus but finds little sympathy.
Achilles presides over funeral games for Patroclus, showing princely dignity and making peace between competitors.
Achilles kills the Amazon queen Penthesilea; in some versions he falls in love with her at the moment of death. He then kills Thersites for taunting him and is purified by Odysseus.
Achilles kills Memnon, son of Eos and Tithonus, leader of the Ethiopians. Memnon's followers are turned into birds.
Achilles is fatally wounded in the heel by an arrow shot by Paris with Apollo's help. His corpse is recovered by Ajax and buried at Sigeum.
Thetis and the Muses mourn Achilles; his bones are mixed with Patroclus' in a golden urn; Thetis gives funeral games.
Achilles' ghost demands the sacrifice of Polyxena at his tomb; Euripides' Hecuba dramatizes this.

myths.n: Odysseus and Ajax Compete for Armor
myths.s: Odysseus and Ajax compete for Achilles' armor after his death, each making a speech.

myths.n: Judgment of the Arms of Achilles
myths.s: After Achilles' death, his armor was awarded to Odysseus over Ajax. Ajax went mad, slaughtered sheep, and killed himself. From his blood sprang a flower with his initials.
Ajax, maddened by losing the armor, killed himself by falling on his sword. From his blood sprang a flower with the letters AI-AI.
The Greeks built a hollow wooden horse, hid warriors inside, and left it outside Troy. The Trojans brought it inside despite warnings, and at night the Greeks emerged to sack the city.

The Greeks sack Troy with the help of hostile gods. Aeneas escapes with his father Anchises, son Ascanius, and the household gods, but his wife Creusa is lost. Venus reveals to Aeneas the divine forces destroying the city.

rel.desc: Aeneas participates in the fall of Troy.
The François Vase depicts scenes from the Trojan War.

myths.s: King Oeneus offends Artemis, who sends a giant boar to ravage Calydon. Meleager gathers heroes including Atalanta to hunt it. Atalanta first wounds the boar, Meleager kills it and gives the skin to her. Meleager kills his uncles in a quarrel, causing his mother Althaea to burn a magical log that ends his life.

rel.desc: Meleager leads the Calydonian boar hunt.
Atalanta participates in the Calydonian boar hunt.
Artemis sent the boar that was hunted.
The François Vase depicts the Calydonian boar hunt.

myths.s: The returns of Greek leaders from Troy, including Agamemnon, Menelaüs, Nestor, Diomedes, Idomeneus, Philoctetes, and Neoptolemus, with various fates: some murdered, some exiled, some founding colonies in Italy. The story of Ajax's death and Nauplius' revenge is included.
Odysseus' visit to the Underworld to consult the prophet Tiresias; he performs a ritual sacrifice and speaks with ghosts of the dead.

myths.n: The Bow and the Killing of the Suitors
myths.s: Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, strings his bow effortlessly and shoots an arrow through twelve axes, then kills the leading suitor Antinoüs and, with Telemachus and servants, slaughters all the suitors. The disloyal servants are hanged, and the goatherd Melanthius is mutilated and killed.

rel.desc: Odysseus is the central figure in the myth of the bow and killing of the suitors.
Penelope is involved in the trial of the bow and the aftermath.
Telemachus helps Odysseus kill the suitors.
Antinoüs is the first suitor killed by Odysseus.
Euryclea identifies the disloyal servant-women.
Medon is spared by Odysseus.
Phemius is spared by Odysseus.
Melanthius is mutilated and killed.

myths.s: The overall narrative of Odysseus' return to Ithaca after the Trojan War, including his encounters with various characters and his eventual reunion with Penelope. The chapter also covers Telemachus' journey to Pylos and Sparta, and the background of Odysseus' parentage.

rel.desc: Laertes appears in the last book of the Odyssey when Odysseus reveals his identity.
Sisyphus is mentioned as an alternative father of Odysseus.
Anticlea is the mother of Odysseus.
Autolycus is the grandfather of Odysseus.
Hermes is the father of Autolycus.
Athena inspires Telemachus.
Nestor is visited by Telemachus.
Menelaüs is visited by Telemachus.
Helen is visited by Telemachus.
Aphrodite is mentioned in comparison to Penelope.
Artemis is mentioned in comparison to Penelope.
Poseidon shatters Odysseus' boat in the background of Pinturicchio's fresco.
Circe meets Odysseus in the background of Pinturicchio's fresco.
Theoclymenus appears in Pinturicchio's fresco.
Eumaeus appears in Pinturicchio's fresco.
Aeolus is the father of Sisyphus.

myths.s: Penelope devises a contest where the suitors must string Odysseus' bow and shoot an arrow through twelve axes. Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, succeeds and then slaughters the suitors.
After stringing the bow, Odysseus, with the help of Telemachus and Athena, kills all the suitors in the hall and cleanses the palace.
Penelope tests Odysseus by asking Euryclea to move their bed, revealing the secret of its construction. Odysseus reacts angrily, proving his identity, and they are reunited.
Autolycus names the infant Odysseus, meaning 'man of pain' or 'hateful', reflecting his future sufferings and causing pain to others.
Athena, disguised as a shepherd, meets Odysseus on Ithaca after his return. They recognize each other's cunning and plan his revenge against the suitors.
Tiresias prophesies that after killing the suitors, Odysseus must travel inland with an oar until he finds people who know nothing of the sea, then make a sacrifice to Poseidon.
Lost epic continuing Odysseus's story after the Odyssey; Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe, travels to Ithaca, kills Odysseus unknowingly, and later marries Penelope; Circe marries Telemachus.
Story of Macareus and Canace, children of Aeolus, who fell in love and had a child; Aeolus forced them to suicide.

rel.desc: Hellen is the father of Aeolus.
Macar is the son of Aeolus.
Sisyphus is the son of Aeolus.
Salmoneus is a son of Aeolus.
Aeolus gave Odysseus bag of winds.
Aeolus is the father of Sisyphus.
Odysseus visits Aeolus, who gives him the winds.
Macareus is son of Aeolus.
Canace is daughter of Aeolus.

myths.s: Phoroneus decided in favor of Hera in the contest for the land between Poseidon and Hera. In anger, Poseidon dried up the Argive rivers.

Perseus, son of Zeus and Danaë, is sent by King Polydectes to fetch the head of Medusa. With help from Hermes and Athena, he obtains magic objects from nymphs, forces the Graeae to reveal their location, and beheads Medusa using a reflective shield. He uses the head to turn Polydectes to stone.

Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus and Cassiepea, is offered as a sacrifice to a sea-monster sent by Poseidon because Cassiepea boasted she was more beautiful than the Nereids. Perseus rescues her and later marries her.

rel.desc: Andromeda is daughter of Cepheus.
Andromeda is daughter of Cassiepea.
Perseus married Andromeda after rescuing her.
Perseus rescued Andromeda from the sea-monster.
Andromeda is the daughter of Cassiopeia.
Andromeda was previously betrothed to Phineus.
Perses is the son of Perseus and Andromeda.

myths.s: Perseus, son of Danaë and Zeus, is sent by Polydectes to fetch the head of Medusa. With help from Hermes and Athena, he obtains winged sandals, a cap of invisibility, a kibisis, and a scimitar. He beheads Medusa, and from her body springs Pegasus.

rel.desc: Perseus is the main hero of this myth.

myths.s: Cepheus and Cassiopeia's boasting angers Poseidon, who sends a sea-monster. Andromeda is chained to a rock as sacrifice. Perseus kills the monster, marries Andromeda, and turns Phineus to stone with Medusa's head. Their son Perses is left as heir.

myths.n: The Origin of Libyan Snakes, the Atlas Range, and Coral
myths.s: As Perseus flies over Libya, Medusa's blood drips and creates poisonous snakes. Atlas is turned to stone and becomes a mountain range. Coral is created when Perseus places Medusa's head on seaweed, which hardens.

rel.desc: Perseus causes the creation of snakes, Atlas range, and coral.

myths.n: Polydectes and Perseus' Return to Argos
myths.s: Perseus returns to Seriphos, finds Danaë and Dictys at an altar. He turns Polydectes and his followers to stone, makes Dictys king, and returns magic objects to the gods.

rel.desc: Perseus returns to Seriphos and turns Polydectes to stone.

myths.s: Acrisius flees to Larissa to avoid Perseus. Perseus accidentally kills him with a discus at athletic games. Perseus then exchanges kingdoms with Megapenthes and becomes king of Tiryns, founding Mycenae.

rel.desc: Perseus accidentally kills Acrisius.

myths.s: Io, daughter of Inachus, is beloved by Zeus, turned into a cow by Hera, guarded by Argus, and rescued by Hermes. She wanders to Egypt, where she gives birth to Epaphus and is identified with Isis.

rel.desc: Io is the central figure in this myth.

myths.s: Epaphus founds cities in Egypt. His daughter Libya gives name to North Africa. His twin sons Agenor and Belus become ancestors of Cadmus, Europa, Minos, Aegyptus, and Danaüs.

rel.desc: Epaphus is the ancestor of many royal lines.

myths.s: Danaüs and his fifty daughters flee to Argos. The fifty sons of Aegyptus pursue and marry them. Danaüs orders his daughters to kill their husbands; all obey except Hypermnestra, who spares Lynceus. The Danaïds are punished in the Underworld.

rel.desc: Danaüs orders his daughters to kill their husbands.
Hypermnestra spares her husband Lynceus.

myths.s: Amymone, a Danaïd, was sent to find water. A satyr attempted to seduce her, but Poseidon saved her and lay with her, causing a spring to burst from a rock with his trident.

Bellerophon, grandson of Sisyphus, was sent by King Iobates to kill the Chimera, a fire-breathing monster. He succeeded with the help of Pegasus, then fought the Solymi and the Amazons, and later killed all ambushers sent by Iobates. He married Iobates' daughter and received half the kingdom.
Poseidon gave the winged horse Pegasus to Bellerophon, but he could not master it until Athena gave him a magic bridle in a dream. He then harnessed Pegasus and performed his labors.
Bellerophon attempted to ride Pegasus to heaven to join the gods, but Pegasus threw him off, and he wandered alone in sorrow, hated by the gods.
In Euripides' tragedy, Bellerophon returned to Tiryns after his labors and killed Stheneboea by luring her onto Pegasus and throwing her into the sea.

rel.desc: Stheneboea fell in love with Bellerophon.
Bellerophon rejected Stheneboea's advances.
Stheneboea was wife of Proetus.
Proetus was husband of Stheneboea.
Bellerophon killed Stheneboea by throwing her from Pegasus.
Stheneboea was killed by Bellerophon.

myths.s: Zeus, disguised as Amphitryon, lay with Alcmena, who conceived Heracles. Hera, hostile, delayed his birth and sent snakes to kill him, but the infant Heracles strangled them. Tiresias foretold his future labors and apotheosis.

rel.desc: Heracles is the central figure in the myth of his birth.

myths.s: Heracles was educated by various teachers, killed Linus with a lyre, and was sent to Mt. Cithaeron. There he killed a lion, entertained by Thespius, and freed Thebes from the Minyans, receiving Megara as wife.

rel.desc: Heracles is the central figure in his early exploits.

myths.s: Hera caused Heracles to go mad, killing his wife Megara and their children. After recovering, he sought purification and was told by the Delphic oracle to serve Eurystheus for twelve years, performing labors to gain immortality.

rel.desc: Heracles is the central figure in the madness myth.
Hera caused the madness of Heracles.

myths.s: Heracles performed twelve labors for Eurystheus: Nemean Lion, Lernaean Hydra, Cerynean Hind, Erymanthian Boar, Augean Stables, Stymphalian Birds, Cretan Bull, Mares of Diomedes, Girdle of Hippolyta, Cattle of Geryon, Apples of the Hesperides, and Cerberus. The first six were in the Peloponnese, the last six elsewhere.

rel.desc: Heracles performed the Twelve Labors.

myths.s: Heracles performed twelve labors for King Eurystheus, including the Nemean Lion, Lernaean Hydra, Stymphalian Birds, Cretan Bull, Mares of Diomedes, Girdle of Hippolyta, Cattle of Geryon, Apples of the Hesperides, Cerberus, and Augean Stables. The labors are depicted on the metopes of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia.
Heracles caught the Cretan Bull that Minos had refused to sacrifice to Poseidon and brought it to Eurystheus. The bull was later released and eventually caught by Theseus at Marathon.

Heracles captured the man-eating mares of Diomedes, son of Ares, and tamed them by feeding them Diomedes himself. He then took them to Argos. On the way, he restored Alcestis to her husband Admetus by wrestling Thanatos.

Heracles was sent to fetch the magical girdle of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons. He killed her in battle and took the girdle. On his return, he rescued Hesione from a sea-monster at Troy and later sacked Troy after being cheated by Laomedon.

Heracles traveled to the island of Erythia to fetch the cattle of the three-bodied monster Geryon. He killed Geryon, his herdsman Eurytion, and the two-headed dog Orthus, and sailed back in Helius' golden cup. He set up the Pillars of Heracles at the Straits of Gibraltar. On his return, he had various adventures including killing Cacus, Eryx, and Alcyoneus. Herodotus tells a version where Heracles fathered Scythes with Echidna.

myths.n: Melampus and the Cattle of Phylacus
myths.s: Melampus helped his brother Bias obtain the cattle of Phylacus as a bride-price for Pero. He was imprisoned but learned from woodworms that the roof would collapse. After being moved, he cured Iphiclus' impotence by finding a knife rust, and received the cattle as reward.

Heracles was tasked with fetching the golden apples from the garden of the Hesperides. He learned the location from Nereus after wrestling him, then either killed Ladon or enlisted Atlas's help to obtain the apples. He also killed Busiris and Antaeus on the journey, and freed Prometheus.

rel.desc: Heracles obtained the apples of the Hesperides with Atlas' help.

myths.s: Heracles' final labor was to capture Cerberus, the three-headed hound of Hades. With help from Hermes and Athena, he wrestled Cerberus in the underworld, brought him to Eurystheus, and then returned him. In Hades, he freed Theseus and saw the ghost of Meleager, who prompted him to marry Deianira.
Heracles, with Iolaus as charioteer and aided by Athena, killed Cycnus, son of Ares, who robbed travelers in Thessaly. He also wounded Ares.

rel.desc: Cycnus is cousin of Phaëthon.
Cycnus was son of Poseidon.
Cycnus was turned into a swan.
Heracles killed Cycnus.
Cycnus is son of Ares.

myths.s: Heracles destroyed the vineyard of Syleus, who forced passers-by to work, and then killed Syleus.

rel.desc: Heracles killed Syleus.

myths.s: Heracles caught the dwarf tricksters Cercopes, but released them after they made him laugh by joking about his sunburned backside.

rel.desc: Heracles caught the Cercopes but released them.

myths.s: While on the Argo, Heracles' beloved Hylas was pulled into a spring by water-nymphs. Heracles searched for him so long that the Argonauts sailed away without him.

rel.desc: Heracles loves Hylas in a male homosexual relationship.
Water-nymphs pulled Hylas into a spring.
Hylas was a companion of Heracles.

myths.s: Heracles attacked Neleus, king of Pylos, for refusing to purify him after the murder of Iphitus. He killed eleven of Neleus' sons, including Periclymenus, but spared Nestor. During this expedition, he wounded Hades and Hera.

rel.desc: Neleus was son of Poseidon and Tyro.
Neleus was son of Poseidon and Tyro.
Nestor was son of Neleus.
Heracles killed Neleus and his sons except Nestor.
Pero was daughter of Neleus.
Heracles attacked Neleus and killed eleven of his sons.
Periclymenus is son of Neleus.

myths.s: Heracles married Deianira after wrestling the river-god Achelous. On their journey, the centaur Nessus attempted to violate Deianira, and Heracles shot him. Dying, Nessus gave Deianira his blood as a love charm.
Heracles fell in love with Iole, but her father Eurytus refused to give her to him. Later, Heracles killed Iole's brother Iphitus by throwing him from a citadel.

rel.desc: Heracles fell in love with Iole.
Iole is daughter of Eurytus.
Hyllus was instructed to marry Iole after Heracles' death.

myths.s: Deïanira, jealous of Iole, sends Heracles a robe dipped in the blood of Nessus. The poison burns Heracles, who in agony kills Lichas and has himself carried to a pyre on Mt. Oeta. He gives his bow to Poeas, instructs Hyllus to marry Iole, and ascends to Olympus to marry Hebe.

rel.desc: Heracles is the central figure in the myth of his death.
Deïanira plays a key role in the death of Heracles.
Nessus' blood is used in the death of Heracles.

myths.s: After killing Iphitus, Heracles is purified but must be sold as a slave. He serves Omphale, queen of Lydia, for a year, performing women's work.

rel.desc: Heracles is the main character in the myth of his servitude to Omphale.
Omphale is the queen who buys Heracles.

myths.s: When the Pythia refuses to answer Heracles, he tries to steal the sacred tripod to establish his own oracle. Apollo wrestles him, and Zeus intervenes with a thunderbolt.

rel.desc: Heracles struggles with Apollo for the tripod.
Apollo wrestles Heracles for the tripod.

myths.s: Prodicus tells a parable where young Heracles chooses between Pleasure and Virtue, opting for the latter.

rel.desc: Heracles is the protagonist of the parable.
Pleasure is one of the choices offered to Heracles.
Virtue is one of the choices offered to Heracles.

myths.s: After Heracles' death, his mother Alcmena and his children were persecuted by Eurystheus. They fled to Athens, where Demophon received them. Macaria sacrificed herself, and Iolaüs captured Eurystheus. In some versions, Alcmena married Rhadamanthys or was transported to the Elysian Fields.

The descendants of Heracles, led by Hyllus and later Temenus, attempted to reclaim the Peloponnese. After a truce of one hundred years, they succeeded with the help of Oxylus, dividing the land into Sparta, Argos, and Messene. The story explains the Dorian invasion of Greece.

rel.desc: Hyllus led the first attempt to return.
Temenus led the successful invasion.

myths.s: Heracles performed twelve labors for Eurystheus, including slaying the Nemean lion, capturing the Cerynitian hind, and taking the cattle of Geryon. The labors are referenced throughout the chapter.

myths.n: Contest of Poseidon and Athena for Attica
myths.s: Poseidon and Athena competed for possession of Attica. Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident producing a salt spring, while Athena produced an olive tree. Athena won and became the patron of Athens.
Hephaestus attempted to violate Athena; his semen fell on the ground and from it sprang Erichthonius, who was partly serpent-shaped. Athena entrusted him to the daughters of Cecrops in a chest.

Athena gave the chest containing Erichthonius to the daughters of Cecrops, forbidding them to look inside. They disobeyed, saw either snakes or Erichthonius with snakelike body, and driven mad, hurled themselves off the Acropolis.

Hermes loved Herse. Aglauros asked for gold to help him, but Athena filled her with envy. Aglauros tried to prevent Hermes from entering Herse's chamber, and Hermes turned her into a rock. Hermes then lay with Herse, and their son was Cephalus.

Cephalus was tempted by Aurora to test Procris' faithfulness. In disguise he attempted to seduce her, and when she nearly yielded, he revealed himself. Procris fled and joined Artemis, who gave her a hound and javelin. Later reconciled, Procris returned. Cephalus, calling for the breeze (Aura), was overheard and misreported as calling a nymph. Procris spied on him, and he accidentally killed her with the javelin.

Erechtheus defended Athens against the Eleusinians led by Eumolpus, son of Poseidon. With approval of his wife Praxithea, he sacrificed one or all three of his daughters to secure victory. He killed Eumolpus, and Poseidon killed Erechtheus with his trident.
Erechtheus sacrificed his daughters to ensure victory against the Eleusinians. In Euripides' Ion, Creusa says all her sisters were sacrificed except herself, who was a baby.
Tereus married Procne and later violated her sister Philomela, cutting out her tongue and imprisoning her. Philomela wove the story into a tapestry and sent it to Procne. The myth is told by Ovid.

Tereus rapes Philomela, cuts out her tongue, and imprisons her. Philomela weaves the story into a tapestry and sends it to her sister Procne. Procne, in revenge, kills her son Itys and serves him to Tereus. The sisters are transformed into birds, and Tereus into a hoopoe.

Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus, is loved by Apollo and bears Ion, whom she exposes. Ion is saved by Hermes and raised at Delphi. Years later, Creusa and her husband Xuthus consult the oracle; Xuthus is told to greet the first person he meets as his son, who is Ion. Creusa, not recognizing him, tries to kill him, but Athena intervenes and mother and son are reunited. Ion becomes ancestor of the Ionic tribes.

rel.desc: Xuthus is the father of Ion.
Ion is son of Apollo.
Ion is son of Creusa.
Hermes saved Ion at Apollo's request.

myths.s: Boreas, the North Wind, carries off Orithyia, daughter of Erechtheus, to Thrace. She becomes mother of Zetes, Calaïs, Cleopatra, and Chione. Cleopatra marries Phineus; Chione bears Eumolpus to Poseidon.

Erechtheus is succeeded by Cecrops, then Pandion. Pandion is driven out by Metion, flees to Megara, and fathers Aegeus, Pallas, Nisus, and Lycus. After Pandion's death, the brothers recover Athens; Aegeus becomes sovereign.

On his journey from Troezen to Athens, Theseus performs six deeds: kills Periphetes at Epidaurus, kills Sinis at the Isthmus, kills the Crommyonian sow, kills Sciron at the Cliffs of Sciron, kills Cercyon at Eleusis, and kills Procrustes near Athens.

Theseus arrives in Athens. Medea, Aegeus' wife, tries to poison him, but Aegeus recognizes Theseus by his sword and stops the poisoning. Theseus is publicly recognized as son and successor. Later, Theseus kills Pallas and his sons to secure his position.

Theseus captures the bull of Marathon (previously brought from Crete by Heracles) and sacrifices it to Apollo Delphinius. On the way, he is entertained by Hecale, who dies before his return; Theseus orders that she be honored at a festival to Zeus Hecalus.

rel.desc: Theseus captured the bull of Marathon.

myths.s: Theseus deserts Ariadne on the island of Naxos (Dia). Dionysus finds her, marries her, and places her wreath in the sky as the constellation Corona. Various versions exist: Homer says Artemis killed Ariadne; another says she died in childbirth; she was later honored as Ariadne Aphrodite.

rel.desc: Theseus deserted Ariadne on Naxos.
Dionysus found and married Ariadne on Naxos.

myths.s: Theseus forgets to change the black sail to white, causing Aegeus to think he is dead and throw himself into the sea (named Aegean). Theseus becomes king and is credited with uniting Attica (synoecism) and refounding the Isthmian Games.

rel.desc: Theseus became king of Athens after Aegeus' death.

myths.s: Theseus joins Heracles in an expedition against the Amazons and receives Antiope as his share, who bears him Hippolytus. The Amazons invade Attica in revenge but are defeated by Theseus; Antiope dies in the battle.

rel.desc: Theseus fought against the Amazons.

myths.s: Theseus and Pirithoüs, king of the Lapiths, are friends. Theseus helps fight the centaurs at Pirithoüs' wedding. They vow to help each other get wives: Theseus kidnaps Helen (then a child), and Pirithoüs attempts to abduct Persephone. While they are in the Underworld, the Dioscuri recover Helen. Pirithoüs is trapped in Hades; Theseus is freed by Heracles.

rel.desc: Theseus was involved in the adventures with Pirithoüs.
Pirithoüs was involved in the adventures with Theseus.

myths.s: Theseus marries Phaedra, who falls in love with her stepson Hippolytus. When her nurse reveals the secret to Hippolytus, Phaedra hangs herself and leaves a letter falsely accusing Hippolytus of seduction. Theseus banishes Hippolytus and calls on Poseidon to destroy him.

rel.desc: Theseus was involved in the story of Phaedra and Hippolytus.
Phaedra was involved in the story of her love for Hippolytus.
Hippolytus was falsely accused by Phaedra.

myths.n: Theseus as Champion of the Oppressed
myths.s: Theseus gave refuge to exiled Oedipus and, in Euripides' Suppliant Women, championed the mothers of the Seven against Thebes. He attacked Thebes and brought back the bodies of the dead Argive leaders for burial. Evadne, widow of Capaneus, threw herself into his pyre.

Theseus was said to have been an Argonaut and participated in the Calydonian boar hunt. He was driven out of Athens by Menestheus and killed on Scyros by Lycomedes. Later, Cimon brought his bones back to Athens.

Demophon, son of Theseus, loved the Thracian princess Phyllis. He left her, swearing to return, but never did. She hanged herself and became an almond tree. When he returned and embraced the tree, it burst into leaf.

rel.desc: Demophon is the son of Theseus.
Demophon loved the Thracian princess Phyllis.

myths.s: Codrus, the last king of Athens, sacrificed himself for his city. An oracle said the side whose king was killed would win. Codrus disguised himself, provoked enemy soldiers, and was killed, leading to Athenian victory.

rel.desc: Codrus was the last king of Athens.

myths.s: Minos prayed to Poseidon for a bull but kept it, so Poseidon made Pasiphaë fall in love with the bull. Daedalus built a hollow cow for her to mate with the bull, resulting in the Minotaur, kept in the Labyrinth. Daedalus later fled Crete with his son Icarus.

Daedalus made wings of feathers and wax to escape Crete with his son Icarus. Icarus ignored his father's warning not to fly too close to the sun; the wax melted, and he fell into the sea, which was named the Icarian Sea.

Daedalus fled to Sicily and was received by King Cocalus. Minos pursued him and discovered his location by using a spiral shell that only Daedalus could thread. Minos was then killed by Cocalus' daughters in boiling water.
Minos used a spiral shell as a ruse to find Daedalus in Sicily. He asked Cocalus to have it threaded, and when Cocalus returned it threaded, Minos knew Daedalus was there.

An oracle foretold that Althaemenes would kill his father Catreus. Althaemenes fled to Rhodes with his sister Apemosyne to avoid this fate. Apemosyne was seduced by Hermes and killed by Althaemenes. Later, Catreus came to Rhodes and was killed by Althaemenes in a skirmish, fulfilling the oracle. Althaemenes was honored as a hero by the Rhodians.

Glaucus, son of Minos, drowned in a vat of honey. Minos consulted an oracle, which said that the person who could find a simile for a magic calf would find and restore Glaucus. The seer Polyidus likened the calf to a mulberry, found Glaucus' corpse, and later restored him to life using an herb observed from snakes. Minos then forced Polyidus to teach Glaucus the seer's art, but Glaucus forgot it when Polyidus told him to spit into his mouth.

Nisus, king of Megara, had a purple lock of hair that protected the city. His daughter Scylla fell in love with Minos and cut off the lock to betray the city. Minos rejected her, and she was turned into a sea bird (ciris), while Nisus became a sea eagle pursuing her.

Athamas' wife Ino plots to kill his children Phrixus and Helle. Their mother Nephele sends a golden-fleeced ram to rescue them. Helle falls off and drowns in the straits named Hellespont. Phrixus reaches Colchis, sacrifices the ram, and gives the fleece to King Aeëtes.

Jason, rightful heir to Iolcus, is sent by Pelias to retrieve the Golden Fleece from Colchis. He assembles a crew of heroes (the Argonauts) and sails on the Argo. After many adventures, he reaches Colchis and, with the help of Medea, performs tasks to obtain the fleece.

rel.desc: Jason is the central hero of the quest.
Medea helps Jason obtain the fleece.

myths.s: The epic voyage of Jason and the Argonauts from Iolcus to Colchis and back, including adventures at Lemnos, Cyzicus, Cios, with Amycus, Phineus, and the Symplegades.

rel.desc: Jason is the leader of the Argonauts in the quest.
Heracles was an Argonaut but left the expedition early.
Orpheus was an Argonaut, a post-Homeric addition.
Phineus advised the Argonauts about the Symplegades.

myths.s: The Lemnian women, punished by Aphrodite, kill all men on the island except King Thoas, saved by his daughter Hypsipyle. The Argonauts arrive and stay for a year, fathering children. Hypsipyle later becomes a slave nurse of Opheltes.

The Argonauts are welcomed by King Cyzicus of the Doliones. After leaving, they are driven back by winds and in a night battle kill Cyzicus. Later at Cios, Hylas is lost and Heracles leaves the expedition.
The Argonauts encounter the Bebryces and their king Amycus, a son of Poseidon who forces strangers to box. Polydeuces fights and kills him.

rel.desc: Polydeuces fought and killed Amycus in a boxing match.
Amycus is son of Poseidon.

myths.s: The blind prophet Phineus is tormented by Harpies who steal his food. Zetes and Calaïs pursue them until Iris stops them. Phineus then advises the Argonauts about the Symplegades.
Aeëtes sets Jason impossible tasks: yoking fire-breathing bulls and plowing a field. With Medea's help, Jason succeeds and obtains the Golden Fleece.

After obtaining the fleece, Jason and Medea flee Colchis, pursued by the Colchians led by Apsyrtus, whom Jason kills. Their journey takes them to Circe, past Scylla and Charybdis, to the Phaeacians where they marry, then to Libya where they carry the Argo across the desert, and finally to Crete where they defeat the bronze giant Talus.

rel.desc: Jason leads the return journey.
Medea accompanies Jason on the return.

myths.s: At Iolcus, Medea tricks Pelias' daughters into killing him by pretending to rejuvenate him. Jason and Medea are driven out by Acastus and go to Corinth, where Jason becomes king through marriage. Medea resists Zeus' advances and is rewarded by Hera with immortality for her children.

rel.desc: Jason is involved in events at Iolcus and Corinth.
Medea is involved in events at Iolcus and Corinth.

myths.s: Euripides' tragedy focusing on Medea's revenge against Jason after he divorces her to marry Glauce. She kills Glauce, Creon, and her own children, then escapes to Athens.

rel.desc: Hecate is the patron deity of sorceresses like Medea.
Medea helps Jason win the golden fleece.
Medea ruins Jason.
Medea was taken from Colchis.
Medea is wife of Aegeus.
Medus is son of Medea.
Medea attempted to poison Theseus.
Aegeus promised to protect Medea in Euripides' Medea.
Medea helped Jason perform the tasks set by Aeëtes.
Medea is the younger daughter of Aeëtes.
Medea and Apsyrtus are siblings.
Jason married Medea on the island of the Phaeacians.
Medea was priestess of Hecate.
Circe is the aunt of Medea.
Medea contrived the death of Pelias through his daughters.
Hera caused Medea to fall in love with Jason.
Aphrodite caused Medea to fall in love with Jason.
Medea resisted the advances of Zeus.
Hera promised to make Medea's children immortal as a reward for resisting Zeus.
Medea helps Jason obtain the fleece.
Medea accompanies Jason on the return.
Medea is involved in events at Iolcus and Corinth.
Medea was married to Jason until he divorced her.
Medea is the granddaughter of Helius.
Medea sent poisoned gifts that killed Glauce.
Medea's poisoned gifts also killed Creon.
Medea concealed her children in the sanctuary of Hera Akraia.
The sculpture Medea by Paolozzi depicts Medea.

rel.other: Medea Leaves Corinth in a Chariot Drawn by Dragons
rel.desc: The vase painting shows Medea in a chariot drawn by dragons.
Medea begged Aegeus to receive her as a suppliant in Athens.
Eros with his arrows compelled Medea to save Jason.
Jason acknowledges that Medea's love was compelled by Eros, but he does not claim love for her.
Medea's rage and deadly threats against the royal family led to her exile by Creon.
Medea expresses hatred for Jason, calling him 'most vile' and 'hateful to the gods'.
Jason accuses Medea of uttering unholy curses and being crazy.
Medea kills Creusa with poisoned gifts.
Medea kills her own children with a sword.
Medea is granddaughter of Helius, who gives her a chariot.
Medea calls upon Zeus and the justice of Zeus.

myths.s: The play Medea by Euripides depicts the confrontation between Jason and Medea after Jason abandons Medea to marry the daughter of Creon, king of Corinth. Medea, feeling betrayed, plots revenge, ultimately killing Creon's daughter and her own children. The excerpt includes the agon between Jason and Medea, where they argue over past deeds and responsibilities.

Medea, betrayed by Jason who marries Creusa, feigns reconciliation and sends poisoned gifts to Creusa, killing her and her father Creon. She then kills her own children to spite Jason and escapes in a chariot given by Helius.

rel.desc: Horse-drowning sacrifices are offered in honor of Poseidon.

concepts.def: From Greek mythos, meaning word, speech, tale, or story; a traditional story, often about gods and humans.
Stories primarily concerned with the gods and humankind's relations with them.
Also called legend; stories with a perceptible relationship to history, rooted in historical fact.
Synonym for saga; stories with historical roots.
Stories of adventure, often with fantastic beings, where the hero triumphs; primarily for entertainment.
Short, imaginative, traditional tales with high moral and magical content, often for the young.
From Greek aitia (cause); theory that myth explains the origin of some fact or custom.
Origin myth about the creation of the world.
Theory that gods were men deified for their great deeds.
Sustained metaphor where details of a story are symbols of universal truths.
Theory by Max Müller that all myths refer to meteorological and cosmological phenomena.
Freudian concept of a man's sexual impulses toward his mother and hatred toward his father.
Jungian term for a daughter's love for her father and hostility toward her mother.
Mental process consisting of condensation, displacement, and representation.
Jungian concept of inherited psychic tendencies of the race, expressed in archetypes.
Jungian term for traditional expressions of collective dreams, inherited behavior patterns.
Jungian archetype of the female that each man has within him.
Jungian archetype of the male that a woman instinctively harbors within her.
Theory that human avoidance of incest is genetic and epigenetic.
A theoretical approach to mythology that analyzes myths into their component parts, often focusing on binary oppositions and underlying structures.
The theory that myth implies ritual and ritual implies myth, closely connecting myth with religion and ritual.
The theory that myths explain and confirm social customs, beliefs, and institutions by reference to tradition.
The concept that the human mind deals with pairs of contradictions or opposites, and myth functions to mediate between them.
A unit of action or function in a myth, analogous to a morpheme or phoneme in linguistic analysis.
A type of folktale or myth involving a search or journey, often with a specific goal.
A tale that belongs to a general class of stories, often with oral antecedents and structural patterns.
An approach to myth interpretation focusing on the structure of tales, often involving motifemes and cultural/historical dimensions.
The study of myths from different cultures to establish definitions and classifications.
A myth that is transmitted orally, often considered pristine and timeless by some scholars.
A myth that has been written down, often by a specific author, and may have oral antecedents.
An approach to mythology that focuses on the perspective of women and the psychological and social situation of female characters.
A stage in feminist analysis focusing on women's political, social, and economic liberation from and equality with men.
A stage in feminist analysis emphasizing the inherent difference between men and women and the bond between women and nature.
A deconstructive feminist approach focusing on difference, plurality, ambiguity, embodiment, the transitory, and the disruptive.
Theme in mythology involving abduction or sexual violence, often with complex interpretations.
Force symbolized by devotion to Artemis, often associated with women.
Transformation that saves the pursued from a fate worse than death.
Accepted and accommodated as part of life in the ancient world, with no prevailing hostile religious views condemning it as a sin.
Female homosexuality, derived from Sappho of Lesbos; less visible in mythology but present in subtexts.
Greek city-state, fundamental in politics and mores, with marriage and family as core values.

A story that, through its classical form, has attained a kind of immortality because its inherent archetypal beauty, profundity, and power have inspired rewarding renewal and transformation by successive generations.
An emotional and spiritual purging involving the emotions of pity and fear, possibly a goal for all serious mythic art.
Plot; a well-constructed plot with a proper beginning, middle, and end, as defined by Aristotle in his Poetics.
A developed narrative that blends factual and mythical storytelling to provide insight into Greek interpretations of god and fate.
A distinct literary form developed by Plato, using myth for didactic purposes, such as the myth of Er about the soul and afterlife.
Late compilers of handbooks of mythology, such as Apollodorus, Pausanias, Hyginus, and Fulgentius.
The original version of a myth (oral or literary and usually hypothetical) sometimes designated as the Ur-myth.
Sea-power; Minoan Cnossus was a great thalassocracy.
Maze-like structure; originally may have meant 'home of the double ax'.
Double ax, a sacred symbol in Minoan religion.
Bronze Age civilization of Crete, named after King Minos.
Late Bronze Age civilization of mainland Greece, centered at Mycenae.
Bronze Age culture of the Cyclades islands.
Bronze Age culture of mainland Greece (Hellas).
A goddess associated with fertility, possibly worshiped in Neolithic and Minoan religion.
A Minoan goddess depicted with snakes, associated with chthonic powers.
Relating to the earth or underworld.
Civilization that reached its culmination in the Late Helladic period (1600-1100 B.C.); known for Cyclopean walls, tholos tombs, and Linear B script.
Earlier civilization on Crete that influenced the Mycenaeans; worshiped a fertility mother-goddess.
Huge, monumental walls said to be built by the giant Cyclopes; typical of Mycenaean citadels.
Large beehive-shaped tombs built into hillsides; typical of Mycenaean civilization and confirming a belief in the afterlife.
Central room with an open hearth in Mycenaean palaces.
Script used on clay tablets found in Mycenaean palaces; deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952; contains names of Greek deities.
Relating to deities of the earth; concept merged with Olympian religion in Mycenaean times.
Title or epithet for Apollo; early form found in Linear B tablets.
Word meaning 'mistress' or 'lady' in Linear B; suggests worship of a mother-fertility goddess.
An astronomical event where the moon blocks the sun, interpreted by Heraclitus and Plutarch in Homer's text.
An Indo-European language, a dialect of Hittite, used on a seal found at Troy.
Indo-European language of the Hittite Empire, used in diplomatic texts.
A system of writing used for Hittite and other languages.
A complex pictographic script used for Luwian.
A Hittite text mentioning deities of Wilusa, including Appaliunas (Apollo).
Hittite name for a city probably identified with Troy.
The meter of epic poetry, used in the Iliad and Odyssey, conducive to retention of historical fact and oral recitation.
Debates about the authorship, composition, and historicity of the Homeric epics.
Poetry recited aloud, often with musical accompaniment, transmitted by bards like Phemius and Demodocus.
A guild of professional rhapsodists who transmitted Homeric poetry.
Undeciphered script from Minoan Crete, not Greek.
Period of ancient Greek history, with chronology subject to scholarly debate.
Term used in Homer, virtually equivalent to Mycenaean Greeks.
Primordial yawning void or unformed mass from which creation begins; in Hesiod, a gaping void; in Ovid, a crude unformed mass of elements.
A poem by Hesiod describing the genealogy and origins of the gods.
A didactic poem by Hesiod about farming and justice, incorporating mythological stories.
Goddesses of inspiration, daughters of Zeus, who reveal truth to poets.
Primordial god of love and procreation, a potent force in creation myths.
A symbol in Orphic myth from which Eros (Phanes) hatches, representing the origin of creation.
Religious cults, such as Orphism, that involve secret rites and often focus on personal salvation.
Earth, air, fire, and water as primary materials of the universe, theorized by Empedocles.
Ovid's poem focusing on stories of transformation, providing a late Roman mythological survey.
Sacred marriage, a recurring archetype in mythology where sky-god and earth-goddess unite to ensure fertility.
Social system where the female is primary; reflected in the primacy of Gaia in Hesiod's Theogony.
Social system where the male is supreme; reflected in later myths where sky-god becomes dominant.
One-eyed giants, children of Uranus and Gaia, who forged Zeus's thunderbolt.
Hundred-handed, fifty-headed giants, children of Uranus and Gaia.
Daughters and sons of Oceanus and Tethys, spirits of rivers, waters, and springs.
Twelve children of Uranus and Gaia, deifications of natural aspects, important for their progeny.
Dread river of the Underworld, used for solemn oaths by the gods.
Food of the gods, given to Tithonus by Eos.
Divine drink, shed by Helius on Leucothoë's corpse to create the frankincense tree.
Freudian concept of male unconscious fear of being deprived of sexual potency, stemming from guilt over hatred of father and desire for mother.
Mythical period of peace and prosperity under Cronus' rule.
Union of sky and earth deities, reenacted by Cronus and Rhea.
Myth that explains the origin of a practice, natural phenomenon, or institution.
The ten-year war between Zeus and the Olympians against Cronus and the Titans.
The battle between the Olympian gods and the giants (Gegeneis) born from Earth.
Earthborn giants produced by Ge to challenge the gods.
Second age; humans were foolish and impious, destroyed by Zeus.
Fourth age; demigods who fought at Thebes and Troy; some dwell in the Islands of the Blessed.
Fifth and current age; characterized by toil, wickedness, and eventual destruction by Zeus.
Sculptural style characterized by melodramatic, emotional intensity, contrasting with classical restraint.
A later misinterpretation of Pandora's jar (pithos) as a box (pyxis), popularized by Erasmus in 1508.
The only thing remaining in Pandora's jar after evils escape; its nature is ambiguous—either a blessing or a curse.
Hopes given by Prometheus to mortals to prevent them from foreseeing their fate, as described in Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound.
Archetypal motif of a younger god overthrowing an older one to gain power, seen in Greek and Near Eastern myths.
Universal myth motif of a great flood sent by gods to punish humanity, with a few survivors repopulating the earth.
Motif of a god or hero who grows up in nature and overcomes challenges to achieve power.
Archetypal hero or god who slays a dragon, symbolizing triumph over chaos.
Babylonian Epic of Creation, named after its opening words 'When on high...'.
Temple tower characteristic of Mesopotamian religious architecture.
A shield with miraculous protective powers, originally a shepherd's cloak, associated with Zeus.
Principal athletic festival in the ancient world, reorganized in 776 BCE, said to have been founded by Heracles.
Dominant matriarchal mysteries associated with Demeter, refusing to submit to patriarchy.
A place or priestess through which a god gives prophetic responses, often through omens or inspired speech.
A hero associated with the underworld and fertility, often consulted in subterranean settings.
In Athenian pederastic relationships, the older active lover.
In Athenian pederastic relationships, the younger passive beloved.
An entourage of satyrs and maenads accompanying Dionysus.
A relatively late composition invoking Ares with astrological reference to the planet Mars, portraying him as a complex god providing courage.

Abstract concept of fate, often singular, closely linked to Luck (Tyche) and Necessity (Ananke). The relation of gods to destiny is variously depicted; sometimes Zeus is supreme, other times even Zeus must bow to Fate.
The three Fates (Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos) who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life, determining destiny.
System of dating by the Olympic Games, celebrated every four years after 776 BC.
A festival to which all Hellenes came, such as the Olympic Games and the Pythian Games at Delphi.
Conception of deities as human in form and character.
Substance clearer than blood flowing in gods' veins.
Offspring of a god and a mortal, with limited powers and mortal.
Mortal honored with cult after death, associated with chthonic powers.
Belief in many gods, expansive and able to incorporate new divinities.
Belief in one supreme god, emerging within Greek polytheism.
Greek variety emphasizing human potential and achievement.
Force to which even Zeus may be subject.
Dangerous pride or arrogance that leads to downfall; a theme in Greek tragedy.
Divine retribution or vengeance against hubris.
Concept of a deity who is envious of human happiness and causes trouble.
Ritual cleansing of a murderer, performed by Croesus for Adrastus.
Goddess of doom and destruction, associated with Atys.
Another name for Nemesis, meaning 'necessity'.
Sacred choral song performed in honor of Dionysus.
Sacrifice of a hundred cattle.
Annual festival honoring Athena Polias, depicted on the Parthenon frieze.
General Greek term for 'festival', derived from word for 'banquet'.
First month of the Attic year, during which Hecatombaia and Panathenaea were held.
Month during which Anthesteria festival was celebrated.
Spring festival in honor of Dionysus, celebrating new wine, with elements of death and rebirth.
Festival in honor of Artemis.
Women's festival in honor of Demeter.
Festival established in 6th century B.C. in Athens, where tragedies and comedies were performed in honor of Dionysus.
Cult honoring heroes or chthonic powers, with rituals differing from Olympian worship (e.g., blood poured on ground).
A professional diviner who interprets signs from the gods, such as bird flight, dreams, and entrails.
Interpretation of omens, especially from birds, as part of divination.
Examination of animal entrails for divination.
Examination of the liver specifically for divination.
The most significant religious act in Greek ritual, involving the offering of an animal to a deity.
A sacred precinct cut off from the profane world, where sacrifices are performed.
The ritual cry uttered by women at the climax of a sacrifice, expressing joy or emotional release.
The internal organs of a sacrificial animal, roasted and eaten by important participants.
Greek philosopher and successor of Aristotle who attributed three functions to sacrifice: to honor the god, to give thanks, and to persuade the god to grant a blessing.
Anthropologist who argued that sacrificial ritual elements trace back to preagricultural hunting practices and aimed to allay fear and anxiety at killing an animal.
Scholar who interpreted sacrificial ritual as a festive celebration establishing social and religious hierarchy and cohesion.
Epithet of Poseidon, referring to his power to cause earthquakes.
Three-pronged fork, symbol and weapon of Poseidon.
A wooden image of Pallas, decked with the aegis, that fell to Troy and was tied to the city's destiny.
Prize amphora filled with oil, depicting Athena in war gear, awarded at the Panathenaic games.
Ceremonial robe presented to the priestess of Athena during the Panathenaea.
Major fragments of the Parthenon pediments and friezes housed in the British Museum.
Excellence or virtue, especially in the context of a woman's skill in weaving or a man's in war.
Homeric epithet for Athena meaning 'gray-eyed' or 'owl-eyed'.
Art movement in late 19th-century Vienna that sought to break from traditional art forms.
Festival in Athens honoring Athena, with contests and prizes.
Celestial Aphrodite, sprung from Uranus alone; represents ethereal, spiritual love.
Common Aphrodite, sprung from Zeus and Dione; represents physical, profane love.
Distinction between spiritual (Urania) and physical (Pandemos) love; a profound archetype.
Practice of temple harlots in honor of Aphrodite; evidence lacking for widespread occurrence.
Archetypal mother goddess whose lover dies and is reborn, representing vegetation cycles.
19th-century artistic movement rejecting academic conventions, drawing on myth and legend.
Oil used by the gods, perfumed with heavenly sweetness.
Original third sex in Aristophanes' speech, partaking of both male and female characteristics.
In Aristophanes' speech, love is the desire and pursuit of one's other half, aiming to restore the original unified nature of humans.
In Socrates' speech, Eros is described as a daimon, intermediate between god and human, interpreting and conveying exchanges between them.
A philosophical love that inspires the pursuit of wisdom and beauty, transcending physical desire; a love of the eternal and immortal.
A Platonic dialogue in which Socrates and others discuss the nature of love.
A novel by Apuleius containing the story of Cupid and Psyche.
Term derived from Sappho's association with Lesbos, referring to female same-sex love.
Rite performed at Brauron where girls 'played the bear' for Artemis as an initiation before marriage.
Title meaning 'Mistress of Animals,' used for Artemis.
Hatred of women, exemplified by Hippolytus' tirade against women.
Hatred of men, associated with Artemis and the Amazons.
Greek concept meaning good sense, self-control, and moderation; translated as 'to be temperate' in the text.
A god appearing by machine to resolve the plot; Artemis appears as such in the play.
Religious rites, possibly the Eleusinian Mysteries; Phaedra saw Hippolytus participating in them.
A curse granted by Poseidon to Theseus, which Theseus used to cause Hippolytus' death.
Honors bestowed by Artemis on Hippolytus in Troezen, where unmarried girls cut their hair in dedication before marriage.
Rituals for girls' transition to adulthood, often associated with Artemis, such as the 'Bear and Fawn' rites.
A hymn in the Homeric tradition that narrates the birth of Apollo and his establishment at Delos and Delphi.
Maidens who serve Apollo at Delos, known for their singing and ability to imitate dialects.
An archaic stone shaped like an egg, kept in the temple at Delphi, signifying that Delphi was the center of the earth.
Festival held every four years at Delphi, including athletic and intellectual competitions; second only to the Olympic Games.
A three-legged bowl used as a seat for the Pythia during prophecy; symbol of Apollo's prophetic power.
The inner sanctuary of the temple at Delphi where the Pythia prophesied, containing the omphalos.
The title of the priestess of Apollo at Delphi who delivered oracles, often while inhaling narcotic vapors.
A generic term for a prophetess; many Sibyls existed in the ancient world, with the Cumaean Sibyl being among the most famous.
Collections of prophecies of the Sibyls, often consulted by the Romans.
Annual festival in honor of Hyacinthus, celebrated in Sparta with ancient traditions.
Practice of sleeping in a sanctuary to receive divine healing or dreams, associated with Asclepius and Amphiaraüs.
Symbol of the medical profession: a staff entwined by a single serpent, representing rejuvenation and healing.
Winged staff of Hermes with two coiled serpents, symbol of commerce and messengers; sometimes confused with the staff of Asclepius in medical symbolism.
Guild of physicians who considered themselves spiritual children of Asclepius.
Relating to Apollo, representing rational, disciplined, and intellectual aspects of human psychology and culture.
Relating to Dionysus, representing irrational, mystical, and ecstatic forces.
Proverbial Greek maxim associated with Apollo, advocating self-knowledge.
Proverbial Greek maxim associated with Apollo, advocating moderation.
Title of Apollo derived from Pytho, the place where he slew the she-dragon.
Title of Apollo derived from Telphusa, the spring he shamed.
A title of Apollo, associated with healing and victory hymns.
Epithet of Apollo meaning 'dolphin,' derived from his appearance as a dolphin when he first leaped aboard the Cretan ship.
Festival celebrated every ninth year at Delphi commemorating Apollo's slaying of Python.
Practice of using Vergil's works as oracles.
Staff with a serpent entwined; symbol of medicine, associated with Asclepius.
Major religious festivals attended by all Greeks; included Olympian, Nemean, Isthmian, and Pythian Games.
A hymn that tells the story of Hermes' birth and childhood, including the invention of the lyre and theft of Apollo's cattle.
A stringed musical instrument invented by Hermes from a tortoise shell.
A device for producing fire, invented by Hermes.
A meadow associated with the underworld, mentioned in the context of cattle tracks.
Food and drink of the gods, stored in Maia's cave.
A wind instrument invented by Hermes, producing sound heard from afar.
A wide-brimmed hat worn by Hermes, associated with travel.
Sandals with wings worn by Hermes, enabling swift travel.
The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown, often through oracles or omens. Apollo and the holy sisters are masters of divination.
A solemn oath sworn by the gods, often by the river Styx, considered binding.
Square pillar with male genitals and head of Hermes, used as boundary marker and fertility symbol.
Guide of souls to the Underworld, a function of Hermes.
Winged sandals worn by Hermes.
Corpus of works attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, dealing with philosophy, astrology, and alchemy.
A being with both male and female characteristics, as exemplified by Hermaphroditus after his merger with Salmacis.
Stone pillars with a head of Hermes and male genitals, used as boundary markers; their mutilation was a scandal in Athens.
Eponymous nymphs of divining pebbles, described as women with wings and hair powdered with white flour.
Shepherds' pipes of reed, also called panpipes, said to be invented by the god Pan.
Rituals and teachings associated with the worship of Dionysus, involving ecstatic dance and spiritual revelation.
An ivy-covered staff carried by Dionysus and his followers, symbolizing his power.
Female follower of Dionysus, often depicted in ecstatic frenzy.
Male companion of Dionysus, often depicted as half-human, half-goat.
Older satyrs, companions of Dionysus.
A wine cup associated with Dionysus.
Frenzied female worship of Dionysus, characterized by wild dancing, hunting, and raw flesh consumption.
The ritual tearing apart of a victim, such as the goat or Pentheus, in Bacchic rites.
The eating of raw flesh in Bacchic rituals.
Rituals of Dionysus (Bacchus) involving ecstatic dancing, wine, and possession; often performed by women (maenads) in the mountains at night.
Female followers of Dionysus, also called Bacchae, who engage in ecstatic worship.
The eating of raw flesh in Dionysiac ritual, a kind of ritual communion since the god was believed to be present in the victim.
The religious congregation of Dionysiac worship, divided into groups often with a male leader playing the role of the god.
Male companions of Dionysus, part man and part animal (horse or goat attributes); they dance, sing, love music, make wine, and chase maenads.
A festival involving a ritual pursuit of women by night and a return to normal order the next day; connected with the myth of the daughters of Proetus.
A god who dies and is reborn; Dionysus is described as such.
Madness spread by Pan among shepherds.
A nymph who could only repeat the last words spoken; also the phenomenon of sound reflection.
The concept that knowing oneself can be dangerous, as in Tiresias' prophecy for Narcissus.
A psychological term for self-love and self-destruction, derived from the myth of Narcissus.
A lengthy ancient Greek hymn that narrates the myth of Demeter and Persephone, including the abduction and Demeter's stay at Eleusis.
River in the underworld, by which the gods swear unbreakable oaths.
Greek word meaning 'girl,' used as an epithet for Persephone.
Preliminary initiation stage held in Athens in early spring, focusing on purification.
Full initiation stage held annually in September-October, involving processions, sacrifices, and secret rites at Eleusis.
Sacred objects revealed by the Hierophant during the highest rites of the mysteries.
High priest who revealed the Hiera to initiates; title means 'he who reveals the Hiera.'
Sacred drink consumed by initiates during the mysteries, possibly ending a fast.
Sacred vessel for offerings used in the rites of Eleusis.
Bearing of the kernoi, part of the Greater and Lesser Mysteries.
Nighttime celebration following the arrival of initiates in Eleusis.
Sacred wands carried in the torch-lit procession to Eleusis.
Enclosed structure within the Telesterion at Eleusis, possibly containing sacred objects.
Temple of Demeter at Eleusis where the final revelation of the mysteries was celebrated.
Sacred cake offering of barley and wheat, possibly depicted on the Niinnion Pinax.
Covered basket symbolizing secrecy in the ritual, possibly depicted on the Niinnion Pinax.
Religious movement based on the myth of Zagreus-Dionysus, emphasizing immortality and redemption.
Religious cult with secret rites and promises of afterlife benefits, such as the Eleusinian Mysteries.
The highest stage of initiation in the Eleusinian Mysteries, involving further revelation.
Priestly family at Eleusis, descended from Eumolpus.
Priestly family at Eleusis.
An initiate in the Eleusinian Mysteries.
Patron who guided an initiate in the Eleusinian Mysteries.
A women's festival in honor of Demeter, also celebrating Dionysus, characterized by abundant food and drink and ribald behavior.
A ritual invocation of the dead, as performed by Odysseus in Book 11 of the Odyssey.
A plant that grows in the Underworld plain where souls dwell.

Religious practices involving sacrifices and ceremonies for the dead, seen in the Odyssey's Book of the Dead.

Christian concept of final judgment, influenced by classical myths of the Underworld.
A cosmic device by which all revolving spheres are turned, held on the knees of Necessity.
The unified musical harmony produced by eight Sirens perched on the circles of the spindle.
A divinity or guiding spirit chosen by each soul for its life.
The belief that the soul passes into a new body after death; associated with Pythagoras.
Relating to Orpheus or the mystery religion associated with him; involves reward, punishment, and purification.
A sacred branch that Aeneas must obtain to enter the Underworld; sacred to Proserpine.
Goddesses of vengeance, including Tisiphone, who punish sinners in Tartarus.
Paradise in the Underworld for the virtuous and blessed.
The belief that souls are reborn into new bodies after death, as described by Anchises in the Aeneid.
Philosophical and religious beliefs attributed to Pythagoras, including transmigration of souls.
Euphemistic name for the Furies, meaning 'kindly ones', used in Athens after they were appeased.
The court of Athens that decided Orestes' case, representing the new regime of law.
A religious belief system of great antiquity, practiced in northern Asian and native North American cultures; parallels with Orpheus and his religion.
Mystical figure with supernatural powers, entering trance-like states to journey into spirit realm for divination and healing.
Harmonizing of different cults and their myths into some sort of unity; literally 'growing together'.
Rite of initiation into mysteries of Cybele and Attis, involving shedding of bull's blood over initiate in a pit.
Scene depicting Mithras killing a bull, basic to iconography of a Mithraeum.
Female counterpart to hero, often of royal or divine stature, with motifs of seclusion, pregnancy by a god, punishment, and rescue.
The 'sown men' who sprang from the serpent's teeth sown by Cadmus; five survived and became ancestors of Theban nobility.

concepts.n: Iconography of the Rape of Europa
concepts.def: Artistic tradition depicting Europa's abduction, typically showing her either garlanding the bull or riding it through the sea.
Curse invoked by Pelops against Laius for abducting his son Chrysippus, leading to the doom of Laius and his descendants.
Riddle taught by the Muses: 'What is it that has one name that is four-footed, two-footed, and three-footed?' Answer: Man.
Sacred bond between guest and host; Laius violated it by abducting Chrysippus.
Divine laws that compel Antigone to bury her brother despite human law.
Oedipus becomes a hero after death, associated with a locality and performing miracles.
Athletic contests founded by the Seven in honor of Opheltes.
The curse placed by Oedipus on his sons Eteocles and Polynices, which led to their mutual killing.
Divine laws that supersede human decrees, as invoked by Antigone.
The sons of the Seven against Thebes who led a successful expedition against Thebes ten years later.

concepts.n: curse of the House of Atreus
concepts.def: A hereditary curse originating from the murder of Myrtilus and the crimes of Tantalus, leading to a cycle of vengeance and tragedy.
Recurring motif in Greek myths, including the stories of Tantalus, Lycaon, and the banquet of Thyestes, possibly reflecting ancient sacrificial rituals.
Shrine of Pelops at Olympia, located next to the temple of Zeus.
Guilt inherited from murder, central to the curse on the House of Atreus.
Descendants of Heracles who fought against Tisamenus.
Central theme in the Oresteia, involving divine and human retribution.
A literary device where the audience knows more than the characters; used in Sophocles' Electra.
The act of killing one's mother.
Sons of Zeus, Castor and Polydeuces; patron deities of sailors and seafarers, appearing as St. Elmo's fire.
Patronymic for Castor and Polydeuces, meaning sons of Tyndareus (their mortal stepfather).
Electrical discharge seen on ships; associated with the Dioscuri as a sign of deliverance.
A poem retracting a previous statement; Stesichorus' Palinode claimed Helen never went to Troy.
Viewing from the wall; scene in Iliad Book 3 where Helen identifies Greek leaders for Priam.
The set of values and ideals associated with Greek heroes, including honor, glory, and excellence in battle and speech.
The state of being unable to be wounded; Achilles was made invulnerable except for his heel by being dipped in the Styx.
The central theme of the Iliad, referring to Achilles' anger at Agamemnon, which causes countless deaths.
Immortal fame earned through heroic deeds, especially in battle.
Achilles learns compassion through suffering, as seen in the ransom scene.
Pessimistic view that human existence is filled with suffering and that happiness is fleeting.
A battle among the gods, as depicted in the Iliad, highlighting the contrast between mortal suffering and divine triviality.
Greek term for moderate or self-controlled individuals, loved by the gods.
Guinea fowl, into which the women mourning Meleager were transformed.
Epic called Returns, narrating the returns of Greek leaders from Troy; only a brief prose summary and three lines of verse extant.
A rite by which ghosts were summoned and questioned; also the name for Odysseus' visit to the Underworld in Book 11 of the Odyssey.
A magic herb given by Hermes to Odysseus to counter Circe's charms; its root is black and flower white as milk.
Sacred bond of hospitality between host and guest, exemplified by Telemachus greeting Athena.
Epithet of Odysseus meaning 'man of many twists and turns' or 'much-turning'.
Epithet of Penelope meaning 'circumspect' or 'wary'.
Term describing Penelope as 'fitting his heart', a perfect match for Odysseus.
Greek for 'Nobody', the false name Odysseus gives to the Cyclops.
Magic object given to Perseus by nymphs, made him invisible.
Magic sandals given to Perseus by nymphs, allowed him to fly.
Wallet or bag given to Perseus by nymphs, used to carry Medusa's head.
Weapon given to Perseus by Hermes.
Shield used by Perseus to reflect Medusa's gaze.
Recurring story elements in folklore, such as magic conception, villainous king, rash promise, supernatural helpers, etc., found in the Perseus saga.
Greek word for labors, meaning contests undertaken for a prize; in Heracles' case, the prize was immortality.
Side adventure; used to describe the centaur episode during the Erymanthian Boar labor.
Additional adventures or side deeds of Heracles during his labors.
Twelve tasks imposed on Heracles by Eurystheus, including the Apples of the Hesperides and Cerberus.
Theme in Heracles' labors, especially the Apples of the Hesperides and Cerberus, symbolizing overcoming mortality.
The transformation of a mortal into a god, as Heracles achieved after his death.
A concept suggesting Heracles' association with animals and his role in taming them for human use.
Philosophical school that valued Heraclean qualities of endurance and virtue.
The Right Time, personified as a deity favoring Iolaüs in Pindar's version.
Boundary markers set by Heracles at the Strait of Gibraltar, associated with the tenth labor.
A depiction of Heracles as an old man with chains from his tongue, symbolizing rhetoric, used in French political imagery.
Horn of plenty, derived from the horn of Acheloüs.
Sprung from the earth; Athenians claimed to be autochthonous, not descended from invaders.
Oracle of Apollo at Delphi; consulted by Aegeus and by Xuthus and Creusa.
The union of different villages into one political unit with Athens as its center, credited to Theseus.
Athletic games held at the Isthmus of Corinth, refounded by Theseus.
A dance performed by Theseus and his companions on Delos, imitating the windings of the Labyrinth.
An object believed to have magical protective properties; here, Nisus' purple lock of hair was the talisman of Megara.
Name for the Argonauts, referring to their descent from Minyan ancestors; cities like Iolcus and Miletus claimed Minyan descent.
Elements in the Argonautic saga that fit a coherent structure when viewed as a quest.
A teacher of rhetoric known for making the worse argument seem the better; Jason is described as an exemplary sophist.
A person who seeks refuge or protection by appealing to a higher power or authority; Medea becomes a suppliant to Aegeus.

concepts.n: Oath by Earth, Helius, and the gods
concepts.def: A solemn oath sworn by Jason, invoking Earth, the sacred light of Helius, and all the gods.
Concept invoked by Medea, referring to divine justice.
The tree into which Cyparissus was transformed after grieving his stag.
The laurel tree into which Daphne was transformed; sacred to Apollo.
The fruit whose seeds bound Persephone to the Underworld.
