Spring near Corinth where Pegasus stood.
Plain where Bellerophon wandered in sorrow after his fall.
Place in southern Thessaly associated with Heracles' death.
Mountain in southern Thessaly, site of Heracles' death and apotheosis.
Mountain in Arcadia, namesake of the Cerynean Hind.
Boeotian town, kingdom of Thespius.
Mythical garden in the far west, site of the Apples of the Hesperides labor.
Arcadian lake where the Stymphalian Birds flocked.
Island far to the west where Geryon lived.
Ancient city in Spain (modern-day Andalusia) where Heracles sailed with the cattle.
Monuments set up by Heracles at the Atlantic entrance to the Mediterranean, identified with Gibraltar and Ceuta.
Rock of Gibraltar, one of the Pillars of Heracles.
Rock of Ceuta, one of the Pillars of Heracles.
City in Phthia, kingdom of Phylacus.
A garden far to the west where the Hesperides guard a tree with golden apples.
Mountains where Prometheus was chained to a rock; visited by Heracles in some versions.
City; kingdom of Eurytus, father of Iole.
Entrance to the Gulf, identified as 'the Narrows' by the oracle.
City where Temenus crossed into the Peloponnese.
City in Laconia, given to Procles and Eurysthenes.
Region in the Peloponnese, given to Cresphontes.
Region in central Greece, where Aepytus was raised.
Location of Geryon's kingdom and the Pillars of Heracles.
City in France where Henri IV was welcomed as the Gallic Heracles.
Achaean river, namesake of the Cerynitian hind.
Island where the Stymphalian birds were later encountered by the Argonauts.
Village near which Theseus killed the monstrous sow.
Location in the Megarid where Sciron operated.
City where Pandion fled and where Nisus became king.
Region in Asia Minor colonized by descendants of Ion.
River in Athens where Orithyia was playing when Boreas carried her off.
Maze in Crete built to contain the Minotaur.
Attic village where Helen was kept after her kidnapping.
Sea named after Icarus, where he fell.
Island; on the right during Icarus' flight in Ovid's account.
Island; on the right during Icarus' flight in Ovid's account.
City in Sicily ruled by King Cocalus.
The Black Sea, where the main part of the Argonautic saga takes place.
Straits between Europe and Asia (Dardanelles), named after Helle who fell there.
Sea of Marmara, where Cyzicus is located.
City on the Propontis, home of the Doliones and King Cyzicus.
Port on the Asiatic shore of the Propontis where Hylas was lost.
Land of the Bebryces, a Bithynian tribe, where Amycus ruled.
City on the Euxine shore of Thrace, home of King Phineus.
Islands where the Harpies were pursued and stopped by Iris.
Clashing Rocks at the western end of the Black Sea, which the Argo passed through.
Land of the Mariandyni, whose king Lycus received the Argonauts.
River in Colchis up which the Argo sailed.
River near whose mouth Jason killed Apsyrtus.
Lake in Libya where the Argonauts were guided by Triton.
Land of the Phaeacians, where Jason and Medea married.
Shoals off Libya where the Argonauts were stranded.
Modern town in Georgia, corresponding to ancient Colchis.

artworks.n: Snake Goddess from the Palace at Cnossos
artworks.desc: Glazed earthenware figure (faience), ca. 1600 B.C., discovered by Sir Arthur Evans in 1903, now in the Archaeological Museum of Heraklion. Depicts a female with elaborate headdress, flounced skirt, open bodice, exposed breasts, holding snakes.

artworks.n: North Entrance Passage fresco at Cnossus
artworks.desc: Fresco of a bull's head, part of a scene of a charging bull or bull-grappling, reconstructed on site.
Relief of two lions or lionesses flanking a column at the entrance to Mycenae; possibly the emblem of the royal family.

artworks.n: Gold masks from Mycenae shaft graves
artworks.desc: Masks of beaten gold placed on faces of corpses in shaft graves at Mycenae.

artworks.n: Reconstruction of the Megaron at Pylos
artworks.desc: Watercolor reconstruction by Piet de Jong of the megaron at Pylos, showing central hearth and throne position.
A model illustrating the results of Manfred Korfmann's excavations, showing the citadel and lower town of Troy VI.
A small round bronze seal, biconvex, with Luwian inscription, dated to the second half of the twelfth century B.C.

artworks.n: Fresco of a lyre player at Pylos
artworks.desc: A fresco found at Pylos depicting a lyre player, illustrating the role of music in Mycenaean civilization.
Red-figure krater by the Darius painter, ca. 330 B.C., depicting Helius driving his chariot upward out of the sea, with diving boys.
Marble sarcophagus from ca. A.D. 200-220, depicting Selene descending to Endymion, with various mythological reliefs.
Painting from 1614 showing Aurora (Eos) preceding Apollo (Helius) with his chariot and the Hours.
Oil on plaster transferred to canvas by Francisco Goya (1820-1822); depicts Cronus cannibalizing his child; part of Las Pinturas Negras.

artworks.n: Rhea Offers the Stone to Cronus
artworks.desc: Roman copy (c. A.D. 160) of Greek original (4th century B.C.); shows Rhea handing swaddled stone to Cronus.
Painting by Rubens that may have inspired Goya's work.
Chryselephantine statuette of a young god from Minoan Age, found near sanctuary of Zeus Dictaeus.
Relief etching by William Blake, frontispiece to Europe: A Prophecy, depicting Urizen as creator with compasses.

artworks.n: Bronze statue of Zeus from Cape Artemisium
artworks.desc: Bronze statue of Zeus hurling a thunderbolt, ca. 460 B.C., height 82 in., found off Cape Artemisium.
Monumental altar with a 100-meter marble frieze of the Gigantomachy, erected by Eumenes II.
Smaller frieze (58 meters) on the Great Altar of Pergamum depicting the myth of Telephus.

artworks.n: Great Altar of Zeus at Pergamon
artworks.desc: Monumental altar commissioned by Eumenes II, ca. 175 B.C., with a frieze depicting the Gigantomachy, about 400 feet long and 7 feet high.
Detail from the east frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon, between 180 and 159 B.C.; height 8 ft. 2 in. Shows Athena striding right, seizing Alcyoneus's hair, with Nike flying to crown her.
Laconian black-figure cup, ca. 560 B.C., depicting Atlas holding up the heavens and watching a vulture attack Prometheus bound to a column.
Oil on canvas, ca. 1910, depicting Pandora holding her box, framed by jewellike flowers with a leafless tree above.
Oil on canvas by Diego Velázquez; depicts Mercury stealthily approaching Argus as he falls asleep, with Io as a cow in the background.

artworks.n: Zeus and Hera metope from Temple E at Selinus
artworks.desc: Limestone and marble metope from Temple E at Selinus, ca. 470 B.C., portraying the hieros gamos of Zeus and Hera. Zeus sits on Mt. Ida drawing Hera toward him; Hera stands facing Zeus with her veil drawn back, wearing archaic clothing.
Monumental chryselephantine statue by Pheidias, about 42 feet high, seated Zeus holding Nike and scepter with eagle, throne decorated with various myths.

artworks.n: West pediment of temple of Zeus at Olympia
artworks.desc: Depicts the battle of Greeks and centaurs at the wedding of Pirithoüs, with Apollo central.

artworks.n: East pediment of temple of Zeus at Olympia
artworks.desc: Shows the scene before the chariot race of Pelops and Hippodamia, with Zeus central.

artworks.n: Metopes of temple of Zeus at Olympia
artworks.desc: Doric frieze with the Twelve Labors of Heracles, each about 1.6 meters high.
Oil on canvas by Ingres (1811), depicting Jupiter enthroned with scepter and eagle, Thetis supplicating, with Juno partially visible.
Roman copy of a Greek original, Hera carrying scepter and patera, wearing crown and chiton.
Red-figure kylix by the Penthesilea painter, ca. 460-440 B.C., depicting the abduction of Ganymede by Zeus. Zeus holds a stylized thunderbolt and scepter; Ganymede holds a cockerel.
Attic black-figure krater by Lydos, ca. 550 B.C., showing a drunk Hephaestus on a mule, accompanied by a thiasos of satyrs and maenads.

artworks.n: The Finding of Vulcan on the Island of Lemnos
artworks.desc: Painting by Piero di Cosimo (1462-1522), depicting Hephaestus as a boy thrown from Olympus and rescued by Sintian women.
Oil on canvas by Diego Velázquez (1599–1660), depicting Helius telling Hephaestus of Aphrodite's affair with Ares.
Roman copy of a Greek original (possibly by Skopas) of ca. 340 B.C., marble, showing Mars (Ares) unarmed but holding his sword, with Cupid added by the copyist.
Temple completed in 456 BC, housing the statue of Zeus. Its sculptures are discussed in art history.
Attic red-figure amphora by Myson, ca. 500 B.C., depicting Croesus enthroned on a pyre, pouring a libation.
Temple of Athena on the Acropolis, with pediments showing Athena's birth and contest with Poseidon, and frieze depicting the Panathenaea.

artworks.n: Statue of a man on a dolphin
artworks.desc: Statue said to have been dedicated by Arion in the temple of Poseidon at Taenarum.
Red-figure krater attributed to the Kleophon painter or his school, ca. 425 B.C.; depicts a ram led to sacrifice, with altar, officiating priest, water basin, kanoun, bukranion, auletes, and youth.
Red-figure Attic krater, ca. 430 B.C.; depicts a sacrifice scene with Apollo holding a laurel branch, altar, laurel tree, officiating priest, youths roasting splanchna, and kanoun.
Central panel of a large square mosaic of Neptune and the Seasons, mid-second century A.D., diameter 77 in. Neptune dominates with four sea-horses pulling his chariot, with a sea-nymph and a Triton.
Fresco by Raphaël, ca. 1512, in the Sala di Galatea, Villa Farnesina, Rome. Depicts Galatea riding a seashell chariot drawn by dolphins, surrounded by Tritons, lovers, and cupids.
Fresco by Sebastiano del Piombo, painted to the left of Raphaël's Galatea, depicting the Cyclops Polyphemus.

artworks.n: The Triumph of Neptune and Amphitrite
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas by Nicolas Poussin, ca. 1637. Depicts Amphitrite at center in a shell chariot drawn by dolphins, with Neptune in a chariot drawn by sea-horses, surrounded by Nereids, Tritons, and cupids.
Marble sculpture by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, 1619. Depicts Neptune striding forward angrily, supported by Triton blowing his conch.
Monumental gold and ivory statue of Athena by Pheidias in the Parthenon, holding Nike, with aegis, shield, spear, and serpent.
Depicts the birth of Athena from Zeus's head, with Helius's horses rising and Selene's sinking.
Depicts the contest of Athena and Poseidon for Athens.
Ninety-two metopes with reliefs: south (Centauromachy), north (Sack of Troy), east (Gigantomachy), west (Amazonomachy).
Continuous frieze around the cella depicting the Panathenaic procession.
Athenian black-figure amphora showing Athena emerging from Zeus's head, with Hermes, Apollo, Eileithyia, and Ares.
Painting by Velázquez depicting weavers and the myth of Athena and Arachne in the background.
Oil on canvas by Gustav Klimt, 29.5 x 29.5 in., depicting Athena with archaic elements, gold highlights, and a nude Nike.
Marble relief from the Acropolis, ca. 460 B.C., height 21 in., showing Athena without aegis or shield, gazing at a stele.
Interior of a kylix by potter Python and painter Duris, ca. 475 B.C., diameter 13 in., showing Athena pouring wine for Heracles.
Simple temple on a bastion at the entrance to the Acropolis.
Three-sided marble relief (ca. 460 B.C.) showing Aphrodite rising from the sea, attended by two women; also includes a musician and a veiled woman on side panels.
Late second century B.C. marble statue of Aphrodite, half draped; best known Hellenistic representation.
Statue by Praxiteles (mid-fourth century B.C.) that popularized nude female form; survives only in copies.

artworks.n: Venus and Adonis by Paolo Veronese
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 1584. Adonis sleeps in Venus's lap; a cupid restrains a hound.

artworks.n: The Heart Desires by Edward Burne-Jones
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 39x30 in. Pygmalion contemplates creation before a plinth.

artworks.n: The Hand Refrains by Edward Burne-Jones
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 39x30 in. Pygmalion hesitates to touch his statue.

artworks.n: The Godhead Fires by Edward Burne-Jones
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 39x30 in. Venus brings Galatea to life with a touch.

artworks.n: The Soul Attains by Edward Burne-Jones
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 39x30 in. Pygmalion reaches to touch Galatea.
Fresco by Annibale Carracci in the Farnese Palace, Rome, depicting the seduction of Anchises by Venus (Aphrodite).
Oil on canvas by Caravaggio (ca. 1601–1602); depicts a prepubescent Cupid with eagle's wings treading on symbols of human achievement.

artworks.n: Cupid and Psyche by Jacques-Louis David
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 1817; depicts Cupid and Psyche after lovemaking, with Psyche sleeping and a butterfly hovering above; Cupid's expression is that of a satiated conqueror.
Statue of Aphrodite by Praxiteles, modeled on Phryne.

Roman copy in marble of a Greek bronze of the late fourth century B.C.; height 78 in. Artemis appears as huntress taking an arrow from her quiver and as protectress of animals grasping a leaping stag.

artworks.n: Death of the Children of Niobe
artworks.desc: Attic red-figure krater by the Niobid painter, ca. 460 B.C.; height 21¼ in. Depicts Artemis and Apollo killing the Niobids in a rocky landscape.
Athenian red-figure krater by the Pan painter, ca. 460 B.C.; shows Artemis shooting Actaeon as his hounds tear him.
Handle of the François vase by Ergotimos and Kleitias, ca. 575 B.C.; depicts Artemis as Potnia Theron holding a panther and a stag.
Statue of Artemis at Ephesus with a robe of animal heads and multiple breasts.
Alabaster and bronze statue from mid-second century A.D., depicting Artemis with multiple breastlike objects, rows of animal heads, turreted polos, and figure of Nike.

artworks.n: Apulian volute-krater by the Darius painter
artworks.desc: Lower register shows the death of Hippolytus: an old retainer runs behind the chariot, Hippolytus loses control as horses panic at a bull from the sea, a Fury holds a flaming torch. Upper register shows six gods including Aphrodite, Artemis, Poseidon.
Red-figure kylix by the Codrus painter, ca. 440 B.C., 12.8 in. diameter. Depicts Aegeus consulting Themis at Delphi; she holds a phiale and laurel branch, seated on a tripod.

Marble sculpture by Gian-Lorenzo Bernini (1624); height 96 in. Depicts the moment of Daphne's metamorphosis into a laurel tree, with Apollo in pursuit. Inscribed with Ovid's description and two Latin lines by Pope Urban VIII.
Votive relief dedicated by Archinus to Amphiaraüs, depicting the healing process: Archinus asleep, a snake biting his shoulder, and Amphiaraüs tending to him.
Painting by Titian (ca. 1480–1576), 85 × 83 in. Depicts Apollo flaying Marsyas, with a dog licking blood, followers playing instruments, Midas contemplating, and an old satyr with a bucket.

Vault mosaic from a third-century A.D. Christian tomb beneath St. Peter's Basilica, showing Christ with attributes of the sun-god (Apollo or Helius), ascending in a chariot drawn by four white horses, with ivy of Dionysus in the background.

Roman marble copy, possibly second century A.D., of a fourth-century B.C. Greek bronze. Height 94½ in. Apollo strides ahead, left hand would have held a bow. Discovered in Rome before 1509, housed in the Vatican's Cortile del Belvedere.

artworks.n: Apollo from the west pediment of the temple of Zeus at Olympia
artworks.desc: Central figure from the west pediment of the temple of Zeus at Olympia, ca. 460 B.C. Height ca. 120 in. Apollo stands calmly amidst the battle of Centaurs and Lapiths, imposing peace.

Attic red-figure hydria by the Berlin painter, ca. 480 B.C.; height 20 ½ in. Apollo rides over the sea in a winged tripod, as dolphins leap above the waves and fishes and an octopus swims below. He wears the laurel wreath and plays the lyre, while his bow and quiver are slung on his back.
Religious object that decked the temple of Apollo at Delphi; tomb of Dionysus.
Statue by Praxiteles, ca. 340 B.C., height 82 in., seen by Pausanias in the temple of Hera at Olympia. Depicts Hermes holding the infant Dionysus, who reaches for grapes. Made of white Parian marble.

artworks.n: Hermes in Crib with Zeus, Apollo, and Maia
artworks.desc: Black-figure hydria from Caere, ca. 500 B.C., 17 in. in height. Depicts Apollo accusing baby Hermes before Zeus and Maia, with stolen cattle behind a tree.

artworks.n: Hermes (Attic red-figure cup by the Euaion painter)
artworks.desc: Attic red-figure cup from ca. 460 B.C. depicting Hermes with his attributes of petasus, caduceus, and winged boots, wearing a traveler's cloak and bearded.

Bronze sculpture from 1576, height 25 inches. Giambologna combines classical attributes of Hermes (petasus, caduceus, winged sandals) with a nude running figure, a masterpiece of Late Renaissance Mannerism.
Red-figure krater showing a young woman clasping the shoulders of Hermes beside a herm.

artworks.n: Herms. Red-figure amphora by the Pan painter
artworks.desc: Red-figure amphora showing a young man between two herms, touching the god's beard in supplication.

artworks.n: A Hermaphrodite. Roman marble copy of a Greek bronze by Polycles
artworks.desc: Roman marble copy of a Greek bronze by Polycles, with marble mattress added by Bernini. Depicts Hermaphroditus with both male and female attributes.
Statues of Hermaphroditus and hermaphrodites became common in the fourth century and Hellenistic period, executed in realistic, erotic, and unusual styles.
Oil on panel by Peter Paul Rubens (1636), depicting Semele and Zeus under extreme emotion as she dies from Zeus's lightning.

Roman marble sarcophagus (mid-second century A.D.) showing Dionysus on a chariot drawn by panthers, preceded by satyrs, maenads, sileni, and animals. Lid shows scenes of Semele's death, birth of Dionysus, and his nurture by nymphs.
Attic red-figure lekythos by the Alkimachos painter (ca. 460 B.C.), showing Zeus giving birth to Dionysus from his thigh, with Hermes present.
Photograph by George Platt Lynes (1907-1955), depicting the birth of Dionysus from Zeus's thigh with erotic and surrealist aesthetic.
Attic red-figure amphora by the Kleophrades painter (ca. 490 B.C.), showing Dionysus with a kantharos and vine branch, flanked by maenads and satyrs.

Attic black-figure kylix by Nikosthenes, ca. 520 B.C. Depicts Dionysus sitting on a square chair holding a rhyton, with dancing ithyphallic satyrs and maenads, vine-leaves and grapes, and a running winged Gorgon in the center.

Attic red-figure kylix (drinking cup) depicting the dismemberment of Pentheus by maenads, with a satyr observing. On the opposite side, Dionysus enjoys wine to music. On the tondo, a maenad holds a leopard and a thyrsus.

artworks.n: Dionysus and Satyrs (red-figure kylix by the Brygos painter)
artworks.desc: Red-figure kylix from ca. 480 B.C. depicting a Bacchic revel with Dionysus playing a lyre, flanked by two satyrs with castanets. Dionysus is wreathed with ivy; satyrs are balding, snub-nosed, with goat's beard, horse tail and ears.
White-ground painting showing a maenad in motion, holding a thyrsus and a small leopard, with a leopardskin and serpent wreath.

artworks.n: Dionysus and Maenads (black-figure amphora by Amasis painter)
artworks.desc: Dionysus holding a kantharos, saluting two maenads who dance and hold ivy and a small deer.
Depicts Dionysus reclining on a ship with a grape-laden vine around the mast; crew transformed into dolphins.
Attic red-figure krater by the Pan painter, ca. 460 B.C., depicting Pan pursuing a herdsman, possibly Daphnis, with a herm or Priapus in the background.

artworks.n: Echo and Narcissus by Nicolas Poussin
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, ca. 1630, showing Narcissus lying by a pool with flowers, Echo fading in the background, and Cupid with a burning torch.
Marble cult statue from the sanctuary of Demeter at Cnidus, second half of the fourth century B.C., height 58 in. Depicts Demeter seated and heavily draped with solemn gaze.

artworks.n: Hades and Persephone by Gian-Lorenzo Bernini
artworks.desc: Marble statue (1621-1622) depicting Hades seizing Persephone, with Cerberus at lower right. Height 87 in.

artworks.n: Pluto and Proserpina by Jeff Koons
artworks.desc: Stainless steel sculpture brushed with yellow-gold paint, decorated with live flowering plants. Height 129 in. Based on an 18th-century porcelain figurine.
Terracotta plaque from Locri, ca. 460 B.C., showing Hades and Persephone enthroned with emblems: grain, parsley, a cock, a bowl.
Athenian red-figure krater, ca. 440 B.C., depicting Persephone emerging from the Underworld with Hermes and Hecate.
Attic red-figure cup by Makron, ca. 480 B.C., showing Triptolemus with grain, Persephone pouring a libation, Demeter holding torch and grain, and personification of Eleusis.
Red-figure clay votive tablet from ca. 370 B.C., dedicated by Niinnion to Demeter and Persephone, depicting scenes possibly from the Eleusinian Mysteries.

artworks.n: Underworld krater by the Underworld painter
artworks.desc: Apulian red-figure krater, ca. 320 B.C., depicting Hades and Persephone enthroned, Orpheus, Heracles with Cerberus, Sisyphus, Tantalus, and other Underworld scenes.
Painted vase depicting the Underworld, focusing on Orpheus, Heracles, and sinners against the gods.
Fresco cycle in Orvieto cathedral depicting the end of the world, including the assembly of the damned.
Fresco in the Sistine Chapel depicting the Last Judgment.

artworks.n: Aeneas and the Sibyl in the Underworld
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas by Jan Brueghel the Elder (1600); depicts Aeneas with sword and golden bough, with Tartarus fires and monsters.
Watercolor by William Blake (1825-1827); illustration for Dante's Inferno; shows Cerberus with three heads.

Attic red-figure vase by the Amphitrite painter, ca. 460 B.C., depicting Ixion naked, looking toward Hera seated on her throne, with Athena holding the winged wheel, Hermes holding Ixion's left wrist, and Ares holding his right wrist.
Oil on canvas by Eugène Delacroix (1863), depicting Eurydice falling as a companion looks at a snake, with Orpheus approaching with his lyre.
Mosaic from Antioch (second century A.D.), showing Orpheus dressed as a Thracian, sitting on a rock and playing the lyre, pacifying beasts and birds.

Marble relief, Roman copy of a Greek original of the fifth century B.C.; height 46 ½ in.; originally part of a parapet around the Altar of the Twelve Gods in the Agora at Athens; shows Orpheus looking back at Eurydice with Hermes Psychopompos.
Athenian red-figure krater by the Orpheus painter, ca. 440 B.C.; shows Orpheus seated on a rock, garlanded with ivy, singing with a seven-stringed lyre to four Thracians.
Marble relief, second century A.D., showing Mithras plunging dagger into bull's throat; bull's tail changes into ears of wheat; below are scorpion, snake, dog; medallions of sun and moon.

artworks.n: Wall mosaic in cemetery beneath St. Peter's basilica
artworks.desc: Third century A.D. wall mosaic showing vine of Dionysus associated with Christian resurrection.
Second-century sarcophagus decorated with relief showing Dionysus finding Ariadne; found in cemetery beneath St. Peter's.
Limestone metope from Selinus, ca. 540 B.C., showing Europa riding the bull over dolphins.
Oil on canvas, 1559-1562, by Titian, depicting Europa's abduction with cupids and distant companions.
Apulian bell-krater by the Darius painter, ca. 340 B.C., showing Laius abducting Chrysippus in a chariot with gods and others.

artworks.n: Oedipus and the Sphinx (Attic red-figure cup by the Oedipus painter)
artworks.desc: Interior of Attic red-figure cup, ca. 470 B.C. Oedipus, dressed as a traveler, ponders the riddle of the Sphinx, who sits on an Ionic column. The Sphinx is winged, with a woman's head and a lion's body and tail.

artworks.n: Oedipus and the Sphinx by Gustave Moreau
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 1864. The sphinx clutches Oedipus, ready to tear him in pieces, while Oedipus gazes at her intensely. Set in the mountains outside Thebes; includes a column with a serpent and an ancient vase with griffins' heads.
Shows the violence of Laius and the dismay of Pelops and Chrysippus.
Campanian red-figure vase, ca. 350 B.C., depicting Capaneus climbing a ladder with torch and axe, with thunderbolt above.

artworks.n: Etruscan funerary ash urn (Death of Eteocles and Polynices)
artworks.desc: Etruscan funerary ash urn (third to second century B.C.) depicting the fallen heroes with two supporters on each side and a winged female demon Vanth holding a torch.

artworks.n: Lucanian nestoris by the Dolon painter (Antigone Is Brought before Creon)
artworks.desc: Lucanian (South Italian) nestoris by the Dolon painter, ca. 380 B.C., showing Antigone brought before Creon, who is seated on a stool wearing a tiara and oriental headdress, with two guards escorting her.

artworks.n: Apulian red-figure krater by the Darius painter
artworks.desc: Krater depicting a scene from Sophocles' lost tragedy Thyestes at Sicyon, showing Adrastus, Thyestes, Pelopia, and other figures.
Attic red-figure krater by the Dokimasia painter, ca. 470 B.C., showing Aegisthus holding Agamemnon by the hair while Clytemnestra runs in with an axe.
Ca. 370 B.C., showing Orestes clinging to the omphalos in the temple of Apollo, with Apollo warding off a Fury.

artworks.n: Electra at the Tomb of Agamemnon
artworks.desc: Lucanian pelike by the Choephori painter, ca. 350 B.C., depicting Electra mourning at Agamemnon's tomb with Orestes and Hermes.
Athenian krater by the Dokimasia painter, ca. 470 B.C. Depicts Orestes killing Aegisthus while Clytemnestra approaches with an axe and Electra runs in.

artworks.n: The Judgment of Paris by Lucas Cranach the Elder
artworks.desc: Oil on panel, ca. 1528; depicts Paris as a corpulent knight, Hermes aged, and the three goddesses; Cupid draws bow; towers of Troy in background.

artworks.n: The Judgment of Paris mosaic from Antioch
artworks.desc: Mosaic from Antioch, early second century A.D.; depicts Paris, Hermes, Hera, Athena, Aphrodite, Psyche, Cupid, and various animals.
Athenian red-figure krater by Euphronios, ca. 510 B.C.; shows Hypnos and Thanatos carrying Sarpedon's body under Hermes' guidance.

artworks.n: Diomedes and Odysseus Stealing the Palladium from Troy
artworks.desc: Detail from an Attic red-figure amphora by the Tyszkiewicz painter, early fifth century B.C.; Diomedes holds the Palladium.

artworks.n: Achilles and Ajax Playing a Board Game
artworks.desc: Attic amphora signed by Exekias, ca. 535 B.C.; shows Achilles and Ajax playing a board game, partly armed.
Red figure kylix by the Peithinos painter, ca. 510 B.C. Depicts Peleus holding Thetis as she transforms into a lion and snakes.
Oil on canvas by J.-L. David, 1819. Shows Achilles drawing his sword in anger at Agamemnon at Aulis, with Iphigenia and Clytemnestra.
Red-figure lekythos, ca. 430 B.C. Depicts Philoctetes sitting alone on Lemnos with his bandaged foot and the bow of Heracles.

artworks.n: Hector and Andromache by Giorgio de Chirico
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 1917, 35.5 x 23.5 in. Depicts Hector and Andromache as mannequins in a stagelike setting, with baby Astyanax as a steel wedge.

artworks.n: Priam and Achilles (red-figure skyphos by Brygos painter)
artworks.desc: Red-figure skyphos depicting Priam approaching Achilles with gifts; Hector's body under couch.

artworks.n: The Death of Hector (modello by Peter Paul Rubens)
artworks.desc: Modello for tapestry showing Achilles killing Hector, with Athena, shield, and river Scamander.

artworks.n: The Funeral of Patroclus (Apulian red-figure krater by Darius painter)
artworks.desc: Krater showing pyre, Achilles killing Trojan prisoners, and Automedon dragging Hector's corpse.

artworks.n: The Building of the Trojan Horse
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas by Giovanni Domenico Tiepolo, 1773, depicting the construction of the wooden horse with Epeus and Odysseus.
Attic red-figure hydria by the Kleophrades painter, ca. 480 B.C., showing scenes of the sack including Priam, Astyanax, Neoptolemus, Aeneas, and Ajax Oïleus.

artworks.n: The Flight of Aeneas from Troy
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas by Federico Barocci, 1598, depicting Aeneas, Ascanius, and Anchises fleeing Troy.
Marble statue by Gian-Lorenzo Bernini (1618-1619), height 86.5 in. Depicts Aeneas carrying Anchises, with the household gods; Ascanius not shown in detail.

Attic black-figure krater by potter Ergotimos and painter Kleitias, ca. 575 B.C., height 30 in. Depicts multiple mythological scenes including the Calydonian boar hunt, chariot race of Patroclus' funeral games, wedding of Peleus and Thetis, and Achilles pursuing Troilus.

artworks.n: Calypso and Ulysses by Emily Marshall
artworks.desc: Watercolor on paper, 1820–1835; 19 × 24 in. Calypso, in early 19th-century dress, tries to comfort Odysseus as he looks over the ocean thinking of Penelope. River landscape with palm tree.
Proto-Attic vase from Eleusis, mid-7th century B.C.; height 56 in., neck 15 in. Odysseus (white) and companions drive pole into Cyclops' eye; he holds wine cup.
Attic red-figure kalyx krater by the Persephone painter, 440 B.C. Depicts Circe fleeing from Odysseus, who threatens her with a sword; two transformed men approach.
Athenian red-figure stamnos, ca. 450 B.C. Odysseus lashed to the mast hears the Sirens' song; his men row with ears plugged; three Sirens on cliffs.
Red-figure amphora, ca. 440 B.C. Odysseus holds olive branches as a suppliant; Athena stands between him and Nausicaä; clothes hang on a tree.

Fresco by Pinturicchio, later transferred to canvas, depicting Penelope at her loom with Euryclea, Telemachus running to greet her, and Odysseus disguised as a beggar entering. Background shows the ship of the Phaeacians, Odysseus' boat shattered by Poseidon, and Odysseus meeting Circe.

artworks.n: The Return of Odysseus (Homage to Pintoricchio and Benin)
artworks.desc: Watercolor, gouache, and ink on paper by Romare Bearden (1977), part of the Black Odyssey series. Depicts the same scene as Pinturicchio's fresco with black figures, referencing African art.
Attic red-figure skyphos, ca. 440 B.C., depicting Euryclea recognizing Odysseus by his scar, with Penelope at her loom on the other side.
Oil on canvas by Edward Burne-Jones (1888), depicting Danaë watching the raising of her prison.
Oil on wooden shield by Caravaggio (ca. 1598), depicting Medusa after decapitation.
Attic red-figure lekythos (ca. 470 B.C.), showing Danaë and infant Perseus in chest with Acrisius.
Limestone metope from Selinus, ca. 540 B.C., height 58 in. Shows Athena, Perseus, and Pegasus springing from Medusa's body.
Oil on canvas by Titian, 1554–1556, 70½ × 77¾ in. Depicts Perseus with winged sandals and harpe.
Etruscan black-figure hydria from Caere, ca. 530 B.C., height 15¾ in. Shows Perseus with rock and scimitar.
Bronze sculpture by Benvenuto Cellini, 1545–1553, in Loggia dei Lanzi, Florence. Perseus holds Medusa's head.
Oil on canvas by Edward Burne-Jones, 1887, 60½ × 50¾ in. Part of Perseus cycle; shows Perseus and Andromeda looking at Medusa's reflection.

artworks.n: Bellerophon and the Chimera (Byzantine ivory plaque)
artworks.desc: Byzantine ivory plaque, fifth century; 8 ½ × 3 ½ in. Bellerophon rides on Pegasus to the right and thrusts his lance into the lion's mouth, as the monster collapses on its front paws. Its serpent-tail twines round one of three trees, and the goat's head melds with another.

artworks.n: Metopes of the temple of Zeus at Olympia
artworks.desc: Metopes depicting the Twelve Labors of Heracles on the temple of Zeus at Olympia.
Oil on canvas by Gustave Moreau (1875/76), depicting Hercules with lionskin, bow, and club fighting the seven-headed Hydra.

artworks.n: Heracles, Assisted by Athena, Cleans the Augean Stables
artworks.desc: Marble metope from the east porch of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, ca. 460 B.C., showing Athena directing Heracles with a crowbar.
Metope no. 10 from the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, ca. 460 B.C., showing Atlas returning with the apples while Heracles holds up the sky with Athena's help.
Etruscan hydria from Caere, ca. 530 B.C.; depicts Heracles presenting Cerberus to a terrified Eurystheus leaping into a jar.
Oil on canvas by J. W. Waterhouse (1896); shows Hylas being lured by seven water-nymphs.

artworks.n: Nessus and Deïanira by Guido Reni
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 1623, depicting the centaur Nessus carrying off Deïanira while Heracles takes an arrow from his quiver.

artworks.n: Heracles and Apollo Struggle for the Pythian Tripod (Attic red-figure amphora)
artworks.desc: Attic red-figure amphora by the Andocides painter, ca. 520 B.C., showing Athena watching Heracles and Apollo struggling for the tripod.

artworks.n: The Death of Nessus (Attic black-figure amphora)
artworks.desc: Attic black-figure amphora, ca. 620 B.C., depicting Heracles killing Nessus with a sword.

artworks.n: The Apotheosis of Hercules by Peter Paul Rubens
artworks.desc: Oil on panel, 1636, showing Hercules ascending from the pyre to Olympus on a chariot.

artworks.n: The Choice of Heracles by Annibale Carracci
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 1596, depicting Heracles choosing between Pleasure and Virtue.
Marble copy by Glycon of an original by Lysippus, found in the Baths of Caracalla, showing Heracles leaning on his club with lionskin draped over a stump.

artworks.n: Hercules Victor (The Farnese Hercules) by Hendrik Goltzius
artworks.desc: Engraving showing Heracles from the rear, clutching the Apples of the Hesperides, with Latin iambic lines describing his labors.

artworks.n: The Discovery of the Infant Erichthonius
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas by Peter Paul Rubens, ca. 1616. Depicts Aglauros opening the basket containing Erichthonius and showing him to her sisters Pandrosos and Herse. Cupid gestures, background includes fountain of Artemis and herm of Pan.
Oil on canvas by Nicolas Poussin, ca. 1630. Cephalus gazes at portrait of Procris held by cupid, resisting Aurora. Background shows Pegasus and river-god.
Oil on canvas by Peter Paul Rubens (1577–1640), 1636–1638, 77 × 105 in. Depicts Procne showing the head of Itys to Tereus, with Philomela behind her.

artworks.n: The Labors of Theseus (Attic red-figure kylix)
artworks.desc: Attic red-figure kylix, ca. 475 B.C., height 5 in., diameter 12¾ in. Depicts the cycle of Theseus' labors on both exterior and interior; interior shows Theseus dragging the Minotaur.

Attic red-figure cup by the painter Onesimos and signed by the potter Euphronios, ca. 500 B.C.; diameter 15¾ in. Depicts Theseus held up underwater by a Triton, with Amphitrite holding a wreath and Athena looking on.
Pencil on paper by Pablo Picasso, 1937, 15 × 22¼ in. Depicts a dying Minotaur seeing itself in a mirror held by a sea-goddess.

Marble sarcophagus, ca. A.D. 180; width 77 in., height (without lid) 20½ in., height of lid 11 in. Shows Dionysus approaching Ariadne on a chariot drawn by a centaur, with various figures including Pan, silenus, cupids, maenads, and Pentheus.

Bronze krater from the second half of the fourth century BC, height 35.5 in, discovered at Derveni in 1962. Reliefs show Dionysus seated with Ariadne, a panther, birds, animals, vines, ivy, maenads, and handles in the form of serpents framing a horned god and Heracles.

artworks.n: The Fall of Icarus by Pieter Brueghel the Elder
artworks.desc: Oil on canvas, 30 x 44 in. Depicts Icarus' legs visible in the sea near a galleon, with a ploughman, fisherman, and shepherd, and a partridge (perdix) referencing Perdix.
Stencil print of a paper cutout, 1947, 16.5 x 25.5 in, from Matisse's Jazz. Shows a black silhouette of Icarus with a red heart against sky and stars.
Terra-cotta relief from Campania, mid-first century A.D., showing Athena helping a workman place a sail, and Argus working on the stern.

artworks.n: Jason Is Disgorged by the Dragon That Guards the Golden Fleece
artworks.desc: Athenian red-figure cup by Douris, ca. 470 B.C.; diameter 11 ¾ in. Depicts Athena watching the bearded dragon disgorge Jason; the fleece hangs on a tree.
Oil on panel by Peter Paul Rubens (1577–1640), 1636, 10 ½ × 11 ¼ in. Jason passes by a statue of Mars with the fleece draped over his left arm, dressed as a Roman soldier.
Welded aluminum sculpture from 1964, height 81 in., depicting Medea with machine parts, implying destructive power.

artworks.n: Medea Leaves Corinth in a Chariot Drawn by Dragons
artworks.desc: Lucanian Calyx-Krater, c. 400 B.C., red-figure earthenware, showing Medea in a chariot sent by the Sun, with Furies, Jason, and mourners.
Campanian red-figure amphora by the Ixion painter, ca. 325 B.C. Depicts Medea thrusting a sword into her son's body, set in a temple with a statue of a god.
